Building Materials You might have heard that carbon dioxide is one of the greenhouse gases that causes climate change. When we burn fossil fuels to create electricity or drive our cars, we put more and more carbon dioxide in the air. Some living things, like coral, actually use carbon dioxide to build structures. Scientists studied how these living things used carbon dioxide and then came up with a way to copy their process. It’s now possible to use some of the carbon dioxide made by burning fossil fuels to create materials similar to concrete that we can use to build new things.
pages.brief: The Moss Landing power plant in California turns carbon dioxide into cement using a process similar to the one corals use to build structures. Coral appears beside the plant, showing how scientists copied a living thing's use of carbon dioxide to make building materials similar to concrete.

pages.text: Why Is Biomimicry So Important? People are great at making the things we want and need. Humans have existed for many thousands of years. During that time, we have gone from living in caves and having to hunt and gather food to sleeping in homes and shopping at stores. Our recent development has forced us to face some pretty tough challenges. One of those is how we go about producing all the things we use.
pages.brief: People are shown making the things they want and need. The scene moves from humans living in caves and hunting and gathering food to people sleeping in homes and shopping at stores, as human development brings tough challenges, including how we produce all the things we use.

pages.text: To make the things we want and need, such as food, homes, plastic bottles, cars, and video games, just to name a few, we use great quantities of resources. We also produce large amounts of waste materials and pollution. Often, the energy used to make and run these things comes from fossil fuels, which cause greenhouse gases to build up in the atmosphere. Also, we create many artificial chemicals that may harm the environment, while the things themselves often end up in landfills when we’re done using them. The buildup of all the greenhouse gases, garbage, and other waste materials is starting to cause problems for us. Our climate is changing because of pollution, and we’re running out of fossil fuels and other resources. Also, our garbage and other waste materials are contaminating Earth in a variety of ways. So what do we do? A truck dumps garbage in a landfill near a small village in the United Kingdom.
pages.brief: A truck dumps garbage in a landfill near a small village in the United Kingdom. Around the scene, people use resources to make food, homes, plastic bottles, cars and video games, producing waste, pollution and greenhouse gases, and the buildup of garbage and other waste is starting to cause problems.

pages.text: One thing we can do is to learn from nature. Nature is great at making the things it needs to survive, too—and it does so very simply and with little waste. A clam creates its shell with nothing but seawater and food. The tallest tree in the world can move water from its roots to its top branches with energy from the Sun and no water pump. Any waste becomes a resource for another organism, such as a dead tree becoming food, shelter, and energy for hundreds of living things. All the different parts of an ecosystem work together in a sustainable way without using up or damaging resources. It has taken many thousands of years to create these sustainable environments. Each living thing—and its adaptations—plays a certain role. Mushrooms and moss grow on a fallen tree. Through the science of biomimicry, we have a chance to see how these sustainable environments survive and how the organisms within them work together. Through them, we can learn and adapt how we live and make the things we use to help solve our challenges and live in more sustainable ways.
pages.brief: Mushrooms and moss grow on a fallen tree. A clam creates its shell from seawater and food, the tallest tree moves water from roots to top with Sun energy and no pump, and waste becomes a resource for other organisms, showing how an ecosystem works together sustainably.

pages.text: Solar Ivy (right) acts like artificial leaves, turning sunlight into energy as a tree does (left). The Future of Biomimicry Artificial Leaves Trees use sunlight to produce energy through a process called photosynthesis. Scientists are working on creating artificial trees with leaves that use sunlight and wind to produce electricity. One day, these trees could produce enough energy to allow us to burn less fossil fuels.
pages.brief: Solar Ivy acts like artificial leaves and turns sunlight into energy, just as a tree does. Scientists are working on artificial trees with leaves that use sunlight and wind to produce electricity, so one day these trees could produce enough energy to let us burn less fossil fuel.

pages.text: This microscopic view of a spider spinning silk (inset) shows how spiders, such as the funnel spider (main), create their webs. Spider Silk Have you ever accidentally walked into a spider’s web? If so, you know how sticky and strong the silk is. In fact, scientists have proven that spider silk is about three times as strong as steel. Now they’re trying to figure out just how a spider makes silk (it’s not a simple process) and then create it themselves. The artificial spider silk would be an incredibly strong, light fabric that’s natural and could have many different uses.
pages.brief: A funnel spider creates its web, and a microscopic view shows the spider spinning silk. The silk is sticky and strong, about three times as strong as steel, and scientists are trying to learn how a spider makes it so they can create an artificial, light fabric with many uses.

pages.text: Antarctic ice fish survive in waters below freezing because of a natural antifreeze in their blood. They can also take in oxygen through their skin! Fish Antifreeze Many species of fish, such as those living in the Antarctic and at the bottom of the ocean, can live in temperatures below freezing. While this extreme cold would kill most creatures, these fish survive thanks to different kinds of antifreezes in their bodies. Scientists are trying to determine how these antifreezes are made and work. If they succeed, they may discover a variety of uses, including organ transplants and ocean exploration.
pages.brief: An Antarctic ice fish swims in waters below freezing. It survives because of a natural antifreeze in its blood and can take in oxygen through its skin; scientists are studying how these antifreezes are made and work, hoping for uses such as organ transplants and ocean exploration.

pages.text: These microscopic views show two types of microorganisms that produce natural plastics. Natural Plastics People use tons of plastic every year, and the way we make plastic uses great amounts of energy and creates huge amounts of waste. However, scientists have found that some kinds of microorganisms make the building blocks of plastics in their cells. If scientists can figure out how these microorganisms begin to make plastics, they can mimic that process and make plastics using less energy and with much less waste.
pages.brief: Microscopic views show two kinds of microorganisms that produce natural plastics. People use tons of plastic every year, and making it uses much energy and creates waste; scientists hope to mimic how these microorganisms make the building blocks of plastics so we can use less energy and create less waste.

pages.text: A chimpanzee and her baby eat medicinal plants. Medicine Other animals have been surviving in the wild for thousands of years, and like us, they sometimes get sick. Yet, they seem to know how to treat their illnesses with native plants and minerals. Many people around the world have also used natural remedies to treat illnesses and injuries for thousands of years.
pages.brief: A chimpanzee and her baby eat medicinal plants. Other animals surviving in the wild sometimes get sick, yet they seem to know how to treat illnesses with native plants and minerals; many people around the world have also used natural remedies for thousands of years.

pages.text: Two children examine a dragonfly. Conclusion We still have a lot to learn about nature and how it can help us create new and better things as well as sustain life—not only ours, but that of every other life-form on Earth. Humans as a species are facing many challenges, some easy and others very difficult. As we try to solve these problems, it might be helpful to take a look outside. The next time you’re playing in a park, walking in a forest, or doing anything in nature, stop and look around. Notice the many living things in your world. Each one has its own special role to play in making every part of the environment work—including yourself. The most interesting and efficient solutions to our challenges may be right under our noses, waiting to be discovered through the science of biomimicry.
pages.brief: Two children examine a dragonfly in nature. Around them, many living things each have a special role in making the environment work, and the scene suggests that the most interesting and efficient solutions may be right under our noses, waiting to be discovered through biomimicry.

books.title: What Is Water Worth?
books.art_why: Real-world water, landscapes, people, and places can be photographed.

pages.text: Russia’s Lake Baikal is the deepest and oldest freshwater lake in the world. It is also the largest by volume but not by surface area; Lake Superior holds that record. Water, Water Everywhere Many of us around the world take water for granted, and why shouldn’t we, when water surrounds us? It comes out of our faucets and collects in puddles on the sidewalk when it rains. Lakes and rivers brim with water. We buy water in bottles and slurp it from drinking fountains. In fact, if we had a glass as big as the United States and filled it with every drop of water on the planet, the glass would have to be 145 kilometers (90 mi.) tall to hold it all. With such an enormous amount of water, you’d think everyone would have enough to drink, but that’s not true at all.
pages.brief: A wide view of Russia’s Lake Baikal, the deepest and oldest freshwater lake, with calm blue water; nearby, people use water from faucets, puddles on a sidewalk, bottles, and drinking fountains. Lakes and rivers brim with water under a rainy sky.

pages.text: A Drop in the Bucket Water is rapidly becoming more precious than gold or oil. The planet simply does not have enough usable water to go around. For one thing, most of Earth’s water is salt water, which we can’t drink or use to water our crops. Only about 3% of Earth’s water is fresh, and most of that is locked away in polar ice caps, glaciers, or underground layers of rock called aquifers. Where’s the Water? Oceans (salt water) 97% Earth’s water Fresh water 3% Ice caps and glaciers 68.7% Fresh water Groundwater* 30.1% Surface water 0.3% Fresh surface water Lakes 87% Rivers 2% Swamps 11% *Groundwater provides 25% to 40% of the world's drinking water, and it provides an even larger percentage of water for growing food. However, groundwater supplies are shrinking.
pages.brief: A split view shows the planet’s water: a vast salty ocean beside polar ice caps and glaciers, with underground rock layers holding groundwater. Below, lakes, rivers, and swamps hold small amounts of fresh surface water. People cannot drink the ocean water, and most fresh water is locked away in ice or underground.

pages.text: Even though the region is water-starved, the people of Saudi Arabia can access water because it is a high-income country. Moreover, water is not equally distributed around the world. Some countries have more water than others, but most have sufficient water to meet people’s needs. What they don’t always have is the means to make that water available to people. High-income countries can tap into hard-to-reach sources of water much more easily than low-income countries, where people often don’t have enough money to dig wells or build dams to create reservoirs. Today, we can only reach and use 1% of Earth’s fresh water. That 1% is under stress owing to three underlying problems: pollution, increased demand driven by the world’s ever-increasing population, and climate change.
pages.brief: In water-starved Saudi Arabia, people access water in a high-income country, while other regions show people digging wells, building dams, and storing water in reservoirs. A small share of Earth’s fresh water remains within reach, with pollution, growing demand, and a warming climate pressing on that supply.

pages.text: Pollution’s Impact Water pollution is a problem on many continents. South America’s Amazon rainforest includes 7 million square kilometers (2.7 million sq. mi.) and is home to about thirty million people and more than thirty thousand plant species. For decades, people have been dumping untreated human waste and toxic chemicals into the Amazon River. These poisons are slowly destroying the jungle’s fragile ecosystem. In other low-income areas where fresh water often goes untreated, disease-carrying organisms grow and make people sick in other ways. Because people lack access to running water or indoor plumbing, bacteria-laden waste then flows into rivers and streams. People use the water in these toxic waterways for drinking, cooking, and bathing. According to the United Nations Development Program, half the world’s hospital beds contain patients sick from waterborne illnesses.
pages.brief: In South America’s Amazon rainforest, people dump untreated human waste and toxic chemicals into the Amazon River, harming the fragile jungle ecosystem. In a low-income area without running water or indoor plumbing, bacteria-laden waste flows into a stream that people use for drinking, cooking, and bathing. Sick patients fill hospital beds.

pages.text: High-income countries such as the United States, where most people have access to clean drinking water, experience other challenges with pollution, the most common of which is agricultural runoff. Every time it rains, chemicals and animal waste from farming are washed into waterways. Additional threats to U.S. waters include an aging sewage treatment system, oil spills, wastewater from fracking for oil and gas, and radioactive waste. The Clean Water Act helps prevent various forms of water pollution. Some administrations have tried to expand its protections, while others have tried to limit them. Do You Know? Worldwide, more people have a mobile phone than a toilet.
pages.brief: In the United States, rain washes chemicals and animal waste from farms into waterways. Nearby, an aging sewage treatment system, an oil spill, wastewater from fracking, and radioactive waste threaten the water. People with clean drinking water use mobile phones, while worldwide more people have a mobile phone than a toilet.

pages.text: Population’s Impact In 2011, humans hit a milestone. On October 30, an infant girl was born in the Philippines: the world’s 7 billionth person. By 2050, experts say that 9.7 billion people will be walking the planet, each looking for food, energy, land, and water. Growing populations reduce the amount of water available for each person. In 1950, the 2.5 billion people on Earth only used a third of the fresh water we use today. Many people thought of water as an unlimited resource. Today, research shows that 1 in 9 people in the world lack safe drinking water. Many live on less than 8 liters (2 gal.) a day. By 2050, more than half of the world’s people will live in water-stressed regions. In Bangladesh, water pollution is caused in part by poverty and in part by overpopulation. Yet its population could balloon to 250 million by 2050—more than 85 million more people than the country held in 2020. High-income countries are far less likely to have to grapple with polluted drinking water because they often have the means to purify their water and dispose of human waste properly. However, population growth in a high-income country can lead to water shortages, too, in part because people in those countries consume more water.
pages.brief: In the Philippines, an infant girl is born as the world’s seven billionth person in 2011. Around her, a growing crowd suggests a planet heading toward 9.7 billion people by 2050. In Bangladesh, many people lack safe drinking water and live on very little water each day, while high-income countries purify water and consume more.

pages.text: Big Population = Big Water Demand In the United States, a four-person family, on average, uses 1,514 liters (400 gal.) of water a day, or roughly 379 liters (100 gal.) per person. This level of use would be sustainable if only a few people were using the water, but more and more people are relying on limited water sources. For example, Los Angeles County’s population is expected to exceed thirteen million by 2050, yet the county can only support one million people on its own water. So what does it do? Los Angeles—and many other cities in the western United States—pull their water from distant rivers. Pulling water is expensive, and there is no longer enough river water to go around.
pages.brief: A four-person family in the United States uses about 1,514 liters of water a day at home. In Los Angeles County, a growing population is expected to exceed thirteen million by 2050, though the county can support only one million people on its own water. Water is pulled from distant rivers.

pages.text: The Impact of Climate Change Climate change is already affecting people around the world by producing extreme weather conditions such as storms and floods. Yet the threat that climate change poses to the global water supply may be the worst threat of all. Scientists predict that by 2050, more than five billion people may face severe water shortages as a result of climate change. Climate change occurs as a result of too much carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. These gases, produced in large part by the burning of fossil fuels, trap the Sun’s heat close to Earth’s surface, much like a greenhouse, which results in an overall increase in Earth’s temperature. That warming, in turn, leads to climate change. The warmer temperatures disrupt the water cycle, which is a delicate balance between evaporation and precipitation. Warmer temperatures increase the rate of evaporation of surface water into the atmosphere, which affects different parts of the world in different ways. Increased evaporation might dry out some areas while producing excess precipitation in others.
pages.brief: Storms and floods show extreme weather linked to climate change. Carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases trap the Sun’s heat near Earth’s surface, like a greenhouse, raising temperatures. That warming disrupts the water cycle, increasing evaporation from surface water. A landscape shows one area drying out while another receives excess rain.

pages.text: Droughts are long periods of abnormally low precipitation that result in a shortage of water. Regions at the highest risk of drought include the Mediterranean and the Middle East. In the United States, most scientists say that climate change is responsible for an extreme drought in the Southwest and California. The drought in the Southwest has been causing problems in the region since 1999. The water level of Lake Mead, on the border between Nevada and Arizona, has plummeted. The lake, which is fed by the Colorado River, is a source of fresh water for twenty-five million people. If rains don’t increase soon, odds are good that desert residents will have to start rationing water. In 2019, Arizona, Nevada, and Mexico agreed to cuts for the first time under a drought contingency plan. A River Runs Dry Nearly forty million people depend on the Colorado River, which now trickles to an end before it can reach the sea.
pages.brief: A long drought dries the Southwest and California, and the water level of Lake Mead on the Nevada-Arizona border has plummeted. The lake is fed by the Colorado River and supplies fresh water to twenty-five million people. The Colorado River trickles to an end before reaching the sea, while desert residents face water rationing.

pages.text: Scientists say climate change is also responsible for the melting of glaciers high in the Himalaya mountains. The glaciers help provide fresh water for 1.5 billion people living in India, Pakistan, and six other Asian countries. In the past, the melting glaciers slowly released water into the tributaries of the Indus, Ganges, and Brahmaputra Rivers. Now the rapid melting of the glaciers is depleting the water supply. At the same time, the increased glacial melt has caused severe flooding along each of the three rivers. As climate change worsens, less water is available for producing energy, raising livestock, and growing crops. Wildlife and natural ecosystems suffer. Arguments break out between cities, states, and even countries over who has the best claim to water. Tensions over water are growing between India and at least two of its neighbors, Pakistan and China. All three are racing to build dams on headwaters in the Himalayas that feed important rivers below. Meanwhile, some countries in Africa argue over who has the best claim on the Nile River. In the Middle East—one of the driest areas on Earth—some experts predict that the next war will be over water.
pages.brief: High in the Himalaya mountains, glaciers melt rapidly and send water into the tributaries of the Indus, Ganges, and Brahmaputra Rivers. The increased melt causes severe flooding, while the shrinking glaciers deplete fresh water for 1.5 billion people. Below, countries race to build dams, and tensions grow between India, Pakistan, and China over water.

pages.text: Solving the Problem So what can we do? Individual efforts to conserve water can have an impact, and states can conserve as well. In 2013, faced with California’s driest year on record, the governor called for a 20% voluntary reduction in water usage. Residents cut back, but when that drought ended in 2017, water use increased again. What Can You Do? • Turn off the water when brushing your teeth. • Take shorter showers (or take baths if you like to linger). • Fix leaks and drips. • Eat less meat (on average, beef requires 125 times more water than the same amount of potatoes). • When you can, buy used or recycled products instead of new ones. • Buy a rain barrel to collect and store water for plants. • If you have a yard, avoid applying chemicals to it. • Plastic pollutes, so reduce your plastic use when you can. (For instance, buy a reusable water bottle instead of purchasing bottled water.) • To help stop climate change, ride your bike, walk, or use public transit.
pages.brief: A person turns off the water while brushing their teeth, takes a shorter shower, and fixes a leak. A rain barrel collects water for plants, and a reusable bottle replaces plastic. In California, residents cut water use by 20% during a drought, but water use increased again after the drought ended in 2017.

pages.text: Competing Water Uses KEY High-income countries World Countries need to help find solutions, too. Workers in Saudi Arabia are converting salt water to fresh water in a process called desalination. The process is expensive, though, and many countries cannot afford to build desalination plants. The island nation of Singapore is purifying wastewater that comes from washing dishes, flushing toilets, and taking baths and showers. Some other countries do this, too, but Singapore obtains one-third of its water this way. Agriculture uses around 70% of the world’s water, but some farmers and ranchers are finding ways to use less. The water saved could instead be used by rapidly growing cities. Solving the planet’s water problem is complicated. Still, we all need to find ways to conserve this valuable resource, not just for our generation, but for the ones yet to come.
pages.brief: In Saudi Arabia, workers convert salt water to fresh water through desalination, an expensive process many countries cannot afford. On the island nation of Singapore, wastewater from dishes, toilets, baths, and showers is purified, supplying one-third of its water. Elsewhere, farmers and ranchers find ways to use less water so rapidly growing cities can share it.

books.title: Mexico
books.art_why: Covers ancient civilizations and the Spanish conquest, so a drawn style suits the historical material.

pages.text: Mexico United States Baja Peninsula Gulf of California GULF OF MEXICO Yucatán Peninsula Mexico PACIFIC OCEAN Mexico City NORTH AMERICA Belize Honduras SOUTH AMERICA Guatemala El Salvador Where Is It? Mexico, a country in the southern part of North America, lies between the United States and Central America. In the north, it shares a border with the United States. In the south, it shares borders with Guatemala and Belize. Mexico also includes some islands. These lie along the western and eastern coasts. To the west of Mexico lies the Pacific Ocean, and to its east lies the Gulf of Mexico. The Gulf of California is between the main land mass of Mexico and the long fingerlike area that juts from its northwest coast, called the Baja Peninsula.
pages.brief: An illustrated map shows Mexico in southern North America, bordered by the United States to the north and Guatemala and Belize to the south. It includes the Baja Peninsula, Gulf of California, Yucatán Peninsula, Pacific Ocean, Gulf of Mexico, Mexico City, islands along the coasts, and nearby Central and South American countries.

pages.text: The center of Mexico City contains the Metropolitan Cathedral. Construction began on the building in the late 1500s. Mexico City, one of the oldest cities in North America, is the capital of Mexico. Home to more than nineteen million people, the city sits in a basin surrounded by mountains. Long ago, the land that the city sits on was a lake bed later drained to build the city. Mexico City’s modern and historic structures make it an interesting combination of old and new. The center of the city contains hundreds of buildings that date as far back as the 1500s. The city also includes floating gardens, which are artificial islands that the Aztecs, a group of ancient Indigenous people, used to grow crops such as corn and beans. Mexico City also contains beautiful parks, including Alameda Park, the city’s oldest. It was created in 1592. Chapultepec Park, the city’s largest park, contains fountains, museums, a zoo, and lakes.
pages.brief: Mexico City sits in a mountain basin, with the Metropolitan Cathedral in its historic center. The city mixes modern buildings with hundreds of structures dating to the 1500s. It also includes floating gardens, Alameda Park, and Chapultepec Park with fountains, museums, a zoo, and lakes.

pages.text: The area that is now Mexico was home to many thriving Indigenous civilizations for thousands of years. In 1521, Spanish explorers colonized Mexico. As a result, about two thirds of Mexico’s people are descended from both Indigenous and European ancestors, and are called mestizos. However, Mexico has one of the most diverse Indigenous populations in Latin America. Groups of Indigenous peoples still make up about one sixth of Mexico’s population. Today, Mexico has a population of more than 120 million people. Most Mexicans speak Spanish, and, in fact, more people speak Spanish in Mexico than any other country. Some people speak Indigenous languages, such as Náhuatl (NAH-wah-tuhl). More than three fourths of the population lives in cities. Mexico’s people have a long and rich artistic history. Ancient Indigenous peoples created stunning works of art that decorated their temples and other buildings. People An ancient Aztec statue of a god stands in the middle of a museum in Mexico City.
pages.brief: An ancient Aztec statue of a god stands in the middle of a museum in Mexico City. The figure represents the long artistic history of Mexico’s Indigenous peoples, whose works of art decorated temples and other buildings.

pages.text: Modern artists have also continued the traditions in painting, sculpture, and architecture. One of the most well-known Mexican art forms is the mural. Ancient Indigenous peoples of Mexico also created beautiful jewelry made of gemstones and precious metals, and the tradition of jewelry making has continued into modern times. Mexico is the world’s leading producer of silver, and many of today’s jewelry artisans work with this precious metal. Sports have also had a long—and serious— history in Mexico. One of the oldest sports played in Mexico, now known simply as the “ball game,” was invented more than two thousand years ago. Some of the stone courts on which the game was played still exist today. Soccer, baseball, and fronton—a game similar to handball—are popular in Mexico today. A player prepares to score a goal for a Mexican soccer team.
pages.brief: A soccer player in a Mexican team uniform prepares to score a goal. The scene includes Mexico’s modern traditions in painting, sculpture, architecture, murals, and jewelry made with silver, plus the old ball game and popular sports such as soccer, baseball, and fronton.

pages.text: Mexico’s Landforms Sonoran Desert Copper Canyon Chihuahuan Desert Baja Peninsula Sierra Madre Oriental Mountains Gulf of California Mexican Plateau Gulf of Mexico Yucatán Peninsula PACIFIC OCEAN Mexico Mexico City Pico de Orizaba Sierra Madre del Sur Mountains Land Mexico is a country of geographic contrasts, with mountains and canyons, deserts and rainforests, mainland, and islands. Mountain ranges occupy the western, eastern, and southern regions of the country. Because Mexico sits at the edge of an unstable area called the Ring of Fire, some of its mountains are volcanoes. In fact, the highest mountain in the country is a volcano 5,700 meters (18,701 ft.) high. The earthquakes that happen around the Ring of Fire can cause terrible disasters. More than nine thousand people lost their lives in the Mexico City earthquake of September 1985, and volcanoes erupted in the 1990s and 2000s.
pages.brief: An illustrated landform map of Mexico shows the Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts, Copper Canyon, Baja Peninsula, Sierra Madre ranges, Mexican Plateau, Gulf of California, Yucatán Peninsula, Pico de Orizaba, and Mexico City. Mountains, canyons, deserts, rainforests, mainland, and islands show Mexico’s geographic contrasts.

pages.text: In opposition to Mexico’s mountains, its canyons and gorges cut deeply into Earth’s crust. Northern Mexico’s Copper Canyon, known for being larger than the Grand Canyon, is 1,400 meters (4,600 ft.) deep in places. The Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts stretch across the northern part of Mexico. The Sonoran Desert has more types of native vegetation than any other North American desert—about two thousand different species. Larger than the state of California, the Chihuahuan Desert is the largest desert in North America. The northern part of Mexico may be dry, but the southeastern part is wet. The area’s rainforests contain thousands of species of animals and plants. Past the eastern coast of the mainland lie Cozumel and Isla Mujeres (EES-lah moo-HAIR-es), two islands known for the brightly colored tropical fish that live in the surrounding ocean waters. Two peninsulas, the Baja and the Yucatán, jut into the oceans on either side of Mexico. The Yucatán Peninsula is made of limestone that in some places has dissolved away over thousands of years to create caves filled with water known as cenotes (sih-NOH-teez).
pages.brief: Copper Canyon cuts deeply through northern Mexico, while the Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts stretch across the north. In the southeast, rainforests are wet and full of animals and plants. Cozumel and Isla Mujeres lie off the eastern coast with brightly colored tropical fish, and the Yucatán Peninsula has water-filled cenote caves.

pages.text: The earliest people in what is now Mexico were Indigenous peoples. Several groups, such as the Maya and the Aztec, developed advanced civilizations with great cities, beautiful works of art, and an accurate calendar that told when to plant crops. About 700 years ago, the Aztec people arrived in central Mexico and established their capital city, Tenochtitlán (tay-nohch-teet-LAHN), on an island in Lake Texcoco. Aqueducts, or waterways, brought water into the city, and canals linked all parts of it. By 1519, the Aztec had built a huge empire of five to six million people. The Aztec thought that because life was the most precious thing people had, it was the most meaningful gift for their gods. As a result, they sacrificed people to their gods. Experts think they may have sacrificed thousands of people every year. In 1519, the Spanish explorer Hernan Cortes arrived in Tenochtitlán, and within two years, enemies of the Aztec had joined with the Spaniards to conquer the Aztec. In 1521, Mexico became a Spanish colony. History The Maya developed an accurate calendar.
pages.brief: The Maya and Aztec built advanced civilizations with great cities, art, and an accurate calendar. The Aztec capital, Tenochtitlán, stood on an island in Lake Texcoco, with aqueducts and canals. The Aztec sacrificed people to their gods, and in 1519 the Spanish explorer Hernan Cortes arrived.

pages.text: When the conquistadores (kohn-kees-tah- DOH-res), which means “conquerors” in Spanish, came to Mexico in the 1500s, they brought with them the diseases of smallpox and measles. The Indigenous peoples had never been exposed to these diseases, and the results were devastating. Scientists think that about twenty million people were living in Mexico at the time of the Spanish conquest. By 1600, barely one million remained. For the next few hundred years, the Spanish ruled Mexico. In 1821, the country won its independence from Spain after years of war. However, freedom did not mean that all Mexican people were fairly treated. Most people were farmers, yet farmers owned almost none of the country’s land. Almost all farmers were poor, and they had few rights. Beginning with the Mexican Revolution (1910– 1920), life started to improve. Today, Mexico is a democracy, and although the lives of many people have improved, the country is still generally divided into two main social classes, the rich and the poor. Leaders of the Mexican Revolution Pancho Villa (left) and Emiliano Zapata (right of Villa).
pages.brief: Spanish conquistadores brought smallpox and measles to Mexico in the 1500s, devastating Indigenous peoples. After Spanish rule, Mexico won independence in 1821, but farmers remained poor with few rights. The Mexican Revolution began in 1910. Leaders Pancho Villa and Emiliano Zapata appear, with Villa at left and Zapata to his right.

pages.text: Landmarks Mexico is a favorite place to travel for tourists from all over the world. Visiting its ancient ruins is one way to step back into the country’s history. Chichén Itzá (chee-CHEN eet-SAH), the best- known Mayan ruin, is located in southeastern Mexico. Chichén Itzá was built at the site of two large cenotes, where religious offerings, including precious gems, and metals, were thrown to honor the Mayan god of rain. The Maya began building the city around the ad 500s, and when it was complete, it included an observatory for studying the stars and planets, a ball court, temples, and a pyramid today called El Castillo. El Castillo, or the Castle, is 24 meters (79 ft.) tall, and each of its four sides contains ninety-one steps. Added together, the number of steps totals 364—the number of days Earth takes to orbit the Sun. By the time the Spanish arrived in Mexico, the Maya had left Chichén Itzá. The jungle covered it for the next three hundred years. In the 1800s, people found the city and began to study it. El Castillo is also known as the Pyramid of Kukulkán. Kukulkán is a Mayan snake god.
pages.brief: Chichén Itzá, the best-known Mayan ruin in southeastern Mexico, was built at the site of two large cenotes. It includes an observatory, a ball court, temples, and El Castillo, a pyramid 24 meters tall with ninety-one steps on each of four sides. A jungle covered it for three hundred years.

pages.text: The Mayan ruins at Palenque (pah-LEN-keh) overlook the surrounding jungle from a mountain forest that provides a home for wildlife such as toucans and monkeys. Palenque contains remarkable architecture, sculpture, wall carvings, tombs of ancient rulers, and even a water system. Writings and symbols carved on tombs and buildings helped scientists understand the history of the city. The ruins of Teotihuacan (tay-oh-tee-wah- KAHN) are located near Mexico City. Scientists are not sure where the people of Teotihuacan lived before they built the city. However, scientists do know that it was one of the largest in the world at the time it was built. Teotihuacan has two main pyramids. The larger is the Pyramid of the Sun; the smaller is the Pyramid of the Moon. The city also includes great temples, palaces, and even apartment complexes. From studying the site, scientists know that like the Aztec and Maya, the people who built Teotihuacan sacrificed people to their gods. The Pyramid of the Sun is the most noticeable feature of Teotihuacan.
pages.brief: The Mayan ruins at Palenque overlook jungle where toucans and monkeys live, with remarkable architecture, sculpture, wall carvings, ruler tombs, and a water system. Near Mexico City, Teotihuacan has the Pyramid of the Sun and Pyramid of the Moon, temples, palaces, and apartment complexes. The Pyramid of the Sun is its most noticeable feature.

pages.text: Folk dancing is a popular pastime in Mexico. Dancers often wear traditional clothing while performing. Conclusion From its Native civilizations, to the Spanish conquest, to revolution and democracy, Mexico is a country with a rich history. Its artistic traditions and ancient ruins tell the long and fascinating story. The country is also one of geographic contrasts. Desert and rainforest, mountain and canyon—all are found in this amazing land.
pages.brief: Folk dancers in traditional clothing perform a popular Mexican pastime. The dancers are the main subject. Mexico’s story includes Native civilizations, Spanish conquest, revolution, democracy, artistic traditions, ancient ruins, and geographic contrasts of desert and rainforest, mountain and canyon.

books.title: Japan
books.art_why: Present-day Japan — bullet trains, Tokyo streets, homes, food and shrines — is a real place that is photographed today.

pages.text: Japan Russia China SEA OF JAPAN (East Sea) North Korea PACIFIC OCEAN South Korea Tokyo Japan YELLOW SEA Japan ASIA Where Is It? Japan is an archipelago, a string of islands that stretches more than 2,400 km (1,500 mi.) just off the east coast of Asia in the Pacific Ocean. Japan is small—smaller than the state of California—and includes four main islands along with thousands of smaller islands. The country’s closest neighbors are China, North and South Korea, and the Siberian region of Russia. The Sea of Japan, also known as the East Sea, lies between Japan and Asia. The East China Sea lies to the southwest of Japan, and the Pacific Ocean lies to the east.
pages.brief: An aerial view of Japan's long chain of islands arcing through the Pacific just off Asia's east coast. Four large islands and thousands of small ones sit in blue water, with the Sea of Japan and the East China Sea to the west and the vast Pacific Ocean to the east, the Asian mainland far beyond.

pages.text: Bullet trains bring people through Tokyo’s busiest train station. The largest island in the chain is Honshu (HON-shoo), which includes more than 80 percent of Japan’s population. The other primary islands are Hokkaido, Shikoku, and Kyushu. The country’s largest cities are on Honshu, with nearly all of them located along the east coast. The capital of Japan is Tokyo (TOH-kee-yoh), also located on Honshu. More than thirty-two million people live and work in this sprawling metropolis. The city—a bustling center for international trade and business—is one of the most populated cities in the world. Millions of people also live in the areas surrounding Tokyo, forming what many call “Greater Tokyo.” People typically travel from these surrounding areas into Tokyo on high- speed trains called bullet trains, as well as on slower trains and subways. The city is the main transportation hub for Japan. It is said that more people pass through the Shinjuku (SHEEN-ju-ku) railway station in Tokyo than any other railway station in the world.
pages.brief: A sleek white bullet train slides into Tokyo's busiest railway station. Crowds of commuters with briefcases wait on platforms, some stepping aboard, others hurrying through the packed concourse. Around the station, the streets of Tokyo stretch away, home to more than thirty-two million people living and working.

pages.text: Although Japan is a small country, it has a population of more than 127 million, with over 90 percent of its people living in urban areas. Many people who live in cities work in banks, restaurants, hospitals, and other service industries. Others work in factories, producing high-tech electronics such as cell phones, computers, and televisions as well as other products, such as motor vehicles and machines. Japan is one of the leading producers of electronics in the world. In cities along the coast, some people work in Japan’s massive fishing industry, which includes one of the largest fleets of fishing ships in the world. Because Japan’s cities are so crowded, many people live in tall apartment buildings. In the suburbs surrounding cities, people typically live in houses and smaller apartment buildings. When space allows, meticulously groomed Japanese gardens appear beside some homes. People In Japan, cell phones are called keitai (KAY-i-tie).
pages.brief: Japanese workers busy in a crowded city: a banker at a counter, a server in a restaurant, a nurse in a hospital, and factory workers assembling televisions, computers and car parts. Behind them rise tall apartment buildings, while in the suburbs a neat, carefully groomed garden sits beside a small house and fishing boats head out to sea.

pages.text: In some Japanese homes, the floors are covered with thick rice-straw mats, called tatami (tah-TAH- mee). It is customary for Japanese people to remove their shoes when entering a home. Some Japanese sleep on thin beds called futons (FOO- tahns) that are rolled out on the floor. The rooms in some Japanese homes are divided by thin paper or bamboo screens instead of walls. Japanese people observe many different rules for manners, such as for greeting people and serving guests. For example, instead of shaking hands when greeting each other, they bow. How many times they bow and how deeply they bow depends on the person’s social status. Japan’s main language is Japanese, the writing of which is very complex. It uses two scripts, known as hiragana and katakana, which each contain about fifty symbols that represent different sounds. Japanese also uses kanji, which are borrowed Chinese characters, and even the Latin alphabet we use in English! Japanese Kanji fire mountain rain.
pages.brief: Inside a Japanese home, thick tatami mats of woven rice straw cover the floor. A thin futon is rolled out ready for sleeping, and paper and bamboo screens divide the rooms instead of walls. At the doorway, shoes have been left, and two people greet each other with a deep bow rather than a handshake.

pages.text: Japan’s Landforms Kyushu Hokkaido Hidaka Mts. Ryukyu Islands Honshu Ou Mts. SEA OF JAPAN (East Sea) PACIFIC OCEAN Japan Japanese Alps Tokyo Chugoku Mts. Mount Fuji Izu Archipelogo Shikoku Mts. Shikoku Kyushu Mts. Kyushu Land Japan is a rugged country covered with lofty mountains and surrounded by water. In fact, most of Japan is mountainous, which is why nearly all of its cities are located in the flat coastal areas. The land on some islands is so steep and treacherous that people cannot live there. The highest peak is Mount Fuji, a volcano on the southern coast of Honshu.
pages.brief: Mount Fuji, a towering volcano on the southern coast of Honshu, rises above steep, rugged mountains. Ridge after ridge of the Japanese Alps and other ranges fill the interior, too treacherous for people to settle, while narrow flat strips along the coast hold the crowded cities and towns where nearly everyone lives.

pages.text: Japan is located in one of the most geologically unstable areas in the world, with more than seventy active volcanoes and one thousand earthquakes annually. An earthquake that occurs along the ocean floor can create a giant wave called a tsunami (tsoo-NAH-mee), which means “harbor wave” in Japanese. Fast-flowing rivers cascade down the mountains of Japan and into the flat areas. These rivers help provide water to the many rice farms throughout the coastal lands. Lakes can be found both near the ocean and in volcanic craters called calderas that have gradually filled with rainwater. Monsoons influence Japan’s climate by causing high winds that can be wet and stormy or dry. Temperatures throughout Japan typically vary widely, with a cooler climate in the north and a warmer climate in the south. Japan’s wide temperature range is similar to the temperature range along the east coast of the United States. Japan’s rainy season in the fall also brings the threat of typhoons. Ishinomaki (ih-SHIH-noh-MAH-kee), a city in northeastern Honshu, was devastated by a tsunami in 2011.
pages.brief: An earthquake along the ocean floor sends a towering tsunami wave racing toward the coast, the kind of wave that devastated the city of Ishinomaki in 2011. Nearby a volcano smokes, fast rivers cascade down mountain slopes to rice farms on the flats, and rainwater fills a lake inside a volcanic crater.

pages.text: Shinto shrine The Japanese call their country Nippon, or “Sun’s origin,” because they once believed that Japan was the first place on which the Sun’s rays shone. The country is also called “Land of the Rising Sun.” The Japanese civilization is thousands of years old, and was heavily influenced by its Asian neighbors to the west. This influence can be seen in various ways, including in its crops. Some historians think the Japanese gained knowledge of growing rice from the Chinese thousands of years ago. In addition, the religion of Buddhism spread from Korea to Japan in the sixth century. However, Japan has also developed its own unique traditions and customs. Shinto is one of Japan’s main religions, and many people observe both Shinto and Buddhist customs. Shinto shrines and Buddhist temples can be found throughout the country. Buddhist temple History.
pages.brief: A Shinto shrine stands beside a Buddhist temple, both quiet places of worship beneath the rising sun. Around them, rice fields spread across flat coastal land, the crop the Japanese learned to grow from their Asian neighbours long ago. Worshippers pass the shrine gate, keeping the customs of two faiths side by side.

pages.text: Japan’s history is rife with conflict over both land and power. However, the emperor of Japan has come from the same family, the Yamato dynasty, for more than two thousand years. It is the oldest continuous monarchy in the world. In the twelfth century, a Japanese warrior seized control of the country. He was the first shogun, or military king. For centuries, Japan was ruled by the shoguns. The shoguns continued to allow the imperial family to serve as emperors even though they had scant power. This time of the shogunates was also the time of the samurai (SA-muh-rye), fierce warriors who followed a strict code of honor. The samurai were also known as skilled fighters. During this era, Japan operated under a system of feudalism in which lords owned areas of land and wielded power over the people living on the land. These peasants had to work for the lord in order to live there. In the nineteenth century, Japan became a democracy in which people elected leaders to the Japanese parliament, called the Diet. Japan still has an emperor today, but since the end of World War II his duties have been ceremonial, not political.
pages.brief: A samurai warrior in armour stands guard, sword at his side, sworn to a strict code of honour. Behind him a shogun, the military king, rules from his castle while the imperial family keeps its palace with little power. Below, peasant farmers work the land owned by their lord under feudalism.

pages.text: Celebrations In Japan, people celebrate many holidays and festivals throughout the year. Among these holidays are ones that celebrate the rice planting, harvest, and the good health of children, and others that honor their ancestors. One of the most important holidays in Japan is the weeklong celebration that leads up to New Year’s Day on January 1. During this week, it’s a common Japanese practice to clean the house and pay any debts. People also send good luck cards to each other, and children receive special New Year’s toys. On New Year’s Day, people often dress in traditional kimonos, eat specially prepared foods, and visit a nearby shrine to pray for good luck for the coming year. Another important celebration is the Lantern Festival, called Obon. Held in the summer, Obon allows the Japanese to honor their ancestors. During the festival, lanterns or candles are lit and set on rivers and lakes to float slowly away. During Obon, lanterns and candles are thought to guide the souls of ancestors back to their resting places.
pages.brief: Families celebrate the New Year in traditional kimonos, eating specially prepared foods and visiting a nearby shrine to pray for good luck. Elsewhere, at the summer Lantern Festival called Obon, small lanterns and candles are lit and set floating on a river, drifting slowly away to guide the souls of ancestors home.

pages.text: Rice is an important part of the Japanese diet. It is sometimes served in small round cakes, called mochi (MOH-chee), as a snack. Japanese people also rely heavily on the surrounding ocean for food and incorporate fish and other seafood into many meals. In cities, sushi (SOO-shee) and sashimi (sah-SHEE-mee), both made with raw fish, are popular fast food choices. Many Japanese believe that food should look just as good as it tastes. Meals are typically served as several different small dishes, including soups and sometimes noodles. Like their Chinese neighbors, the Japanese usually eat with chopsticks, which are long, thin utensils made of wood. The Japanese follow many rules when preparing and presenting certain types of food. For example, one traditional ceremony is centered around serving tea and includes a highly organized and elegant process. This tea ceremony is usually held in a special room created just for that purpose. Food Sushi often consists of a sticky rice mixture rolled around raw fish and vegetables to make a roll.
pages.brief: A Japanese meal laid out in several small dishes: a bowl of rice, mochi rice cakes, noodles, soup and a tray of sushi and sashimi made from raw fish. A diner lifts food with long wooden chopsticks. In another room, an elegant tea ceremony takes place on tatami, the host serving with careful, organised movements.

pages.text: Modern buildings crowd around the edges of the Imperial Palace grounds in Tokyo. Conclusion Japan is a small island country covered with mountains, yet it includes crowded, bustling cities filled with high-tech industries. The land shakes with earthquakes, volcanoes erupt, and typhoons rage, but Japan’s people continue to thrive. Over thousands of years, the Japanese have learned to make the most of the land and waters around them. They grow tons of rice in small areas. They harvest large amounts of fish and seafood from the ocean, too. Timeless traditions and customs mingle with cutting-edge technology, making Japan a place that embraces two worlds—the ancient and the modern.
pages.brief: Tall modern buildings crowd the edges of the Imperial Palace grounds in Tokyo, glass towers rising behind the trees of the old palace. People go about their day below: workers, shoppers and commuters in the bustling capital, while beyond the city, rice fields and fishing boats show the other side of Japan.

pages.text: Population: 127,250,000 Land: 364,485 sq km (226,480 sq. mi.) Capital City: Tokyo Primary Language: Japanese Primary Religions: Shintoism, Buddhism Currency: Yen.
pages.brief: Tokyo, Japan's capital city, seen as a crowded street filled with a huge tide of people. Worshippers visit a Shinto shrine and a Buddhist temple, and shoppers handle yen coins and notes. Beyond the city, green fields and mountains stretch across the 364,485 square kilometres the country covers.

books.title: Kenya
books.art_why: Kenya is a real modern country, so photographs can show its land, cities, people, and wildlife.

pages.text: Kenya South Sudan Ethiopia Lake Turkana Uganda Somalia Kenya Lake Victoria Nairobi EUROPE ASIA INDIAN OCEAN Tanzania Mombasa AFRICA Where Is It? Kenya is a country on the continent of Africa that is surrounded by five other countries. Ethiopia lies to the north of Kenya, and Tanzania (tan-zuh- NEE-uh) lies to the south. West of Kenya is Uganda, while South Sudan borders Kenya to the northwest. To the east is Somalia, and the southeastern coast of Kenya is on the Indian Ocean. The equator runs through Kenya, which means that Kenya does not have seasons marked by changes in temperature. Instead, the amount and duration of rainfall marks the changing seasons. Temperatures do vary, however, with the mountains being cooler than lower places.
pages.brief: A broad view of Kenya in eastern Africa, with Ethiopia to the north, Tanzania to the south, Uganda to the west, South Sudan to the northwest, and Somalia to the east. The Indian Ocean lies along the southeast coast. Lake Turkana, Lake Victoria, Nairobi, Mombasa, and the equator are visible across the country.

pages.text: The capital city of Kenya is Nairobi (nie-ROH- bee), which originated as a railway station during the construction of Kenya’s rail system. Today, more than three million people live there. The city is the industrial center of the country, with factories that make clothing and furniture along with bread, cornmeal, and other processed foods. Because of Nairobi’s location near East African farmlands, crops used as raw materials do not have to travel far to food-processing factories. Nairobi is one of a few capital cities in the world with a wildlife park in its backyard. Nairobi National Park, a large game reserve, lies just 8 kilometers (5 mi.) from the city. Visitors can see lions, giraffes, and various reptiles and birds. One hotel near Nairobi provides a unique experience. At Giraffe Manor, guests can eat breakfast and dinner with Rothschild’s giraffes. The hotel sits on a large sanctuary for this rare species of giraffe. The animals actually stick their heads through the windows! Giraffes at Giraffe Manor often visit in the mornings and evenings.
pages.brief: Nairobi, Kenya’s capital, spreads out as a busy city with factories making clothing, furniture, bread, cornmeal, and processed foods. Nearby, Nairobi National Park holds lions, giraffes, reptiles, and birds. At Giraffe Manor, Rothschild’s giraffes stretch their heads through the windows while guests eat breakfast or dinner at the sanctuary hotel.

pages.text: People More than forty-five million people live in Kenya. It ranks thirty-first in population among the world’s nations and includes more than thirty ethnic groups, or tribes. Almost all Kenyans have African ancestors and speak the language of their tribe in addition to at least one of the national languages, English and Swahili (swah-HEE-lee). English is used in government, higher education, and large business corporations, while Swahili is used in primary schools and many smaller businesses. A small number of Kenyans have ancestors from Europe, Asia, or the Middle East. Many Kenyans enjoy watching and playing football, which is also called soccer. Kenyan runners are renowned for competing in international races and winning gold medals at the Olympic Games. Bao, a popular game played with a wooden board that has small cups for holding seeds or stones, is played by young and old alike. Two young boys play bao, a popular board game in Kenya. Bao means “board” in Swahili.
pages.brief: A lively view of Kenya’s people, including more than thirty ethnic groups and speakers of English, Swahili, and tribal languages. Kenyan football players compete, runners race in international events, and two young boys sit playing bao on a wooden board with small cups for seeds or stones.

pages.text: Sisal plants (main) are crushed and dried to make fibers (inset), which are then woven together. About 75 percent of Kenyans live in the countryside, where most farm to earn a living. They grow food to feed their families, along with crops to sell such as tea, coffee, corn, sweet potatoes, and wheat. They also grow flowers, many of which are used to make a natural insecticide. Another important Kenyan crop is sisal, a type of plant with strong fibers used to make ropes and mats. Tourism is another big source of income for the country, with over a million people visiting Kenya every year. Kangas Cotton is an important crop in Kenya that is used to make clothing such as kangas. Women wear these large, colorful pieces of cloth as shawls, headscarves, and skirts. A woman might also use a kanga to carry her child. Many kangas have a proverb or saying on them, such as this one: “He who digs a well gets himself inside.”
pages.brief: Sisal plants are crushed and dried into strong fibers, then woven into ropes and mats. Cotton grows for kangas, large colorful cloths that women wear as shawls, headscarves, or skirts and use to carry a child. A kanga can display a proverb, such as one about digging a well.

pages.text: Kenya’s Landforms Lake Turkana Chalbi Desert Great Rift Valley Mount Kulai Mount Elgon Kenya Merti Plateau Mount Kenya Lake Victoria Nairobi Loita Hills Yata Plateau Chyulu Range Nyiri Desert Mount Kilimanjaro INDIAN OCEAN Taita Hills Mombasa Land The western part of Kenya contains highlands that are divided by the Great Rift Valley, a 6,437-kilometer (4,000 mi.) crack in Earth’s crust about 50 to 130 kilometers (30–80 mi.) wide. The floor of the valley contains lakes, volcanoes, and deserts. The walls are cliffs called escarpments, which rise up to 2,700 meters (9,000 ft.) above the floor. The highlands are one of two areas that receive enough rain for farming, so most of Kenya’s people live there. Mount Kenya, in the highlands, is the highest mountain in the country.
pages.brief: A view of Kenya’s landforms, with the western highlands split by the Great Rift Valley. The valley floor holds lakes, volcanoes, and deserts, while cliffs called escarpments rise above it. Mount Kenya stands as the country’s highest mountain, and the highlands receive enough rain for farming and settlement.

pages.text: Kenya’s coastal lowlands also receive enough rain for farming. Coconut and cashew crops thrive in this area of the country. White sand beaches and mangrove forests line the coast. Kenya’s deserts, found mostly in the north, are not as large as the Sahara and other African deserts. A few nomadic tribes, who mainly herd sheep and goats, live in these arid areas. At the western edge of these deserts is Lake Turkana, where fossils of the earliest humans have been discovered. Lake Turkana, which used to be named Lake Rudolf, is the largest desert lake in the world. Kenya is famous for its savanna, where large herds of wildebeests, zebras, gazelles, and other animals graze. Grasses on the savanna grow as tall as 1.5 meters (5 ft.), and thorny, flat-topped acacia (uh-KAY-shuh) trees dot the landscape. Kenya’s grasslands are found in the areas west and east of the highlands. Lake Turkana desert savanna.
pages.brief: Kenya’s coastal lowlands show coconut and cashew crops, white sand beaches, and mangrove forests. In the north, nomadic tribes herd sheep and goats in arid deserts. Lake Turkana, the largest desert lake, has yielded fossils of the earliest humans. On the savanna, tall grass and flat-topped acacia trees shelter wildebeests, zebras, and gazelles.

pages.text: History While some of the earliest humans left the region that is now Kenya to settle in other areas, those who remained had little interaction with the world at large until the first century ad, when people from the Middle East and Asia established trade in East Africa. For hundreds of years, people on Kenya’s coast traded enslaved people as well as ivory and other things. People from Europe arrived in Kenya in the late 1400s, and Kenya officially became a colony of the British Empire in 1920. The British angered Kenyans when they gave much of the native land to white people from Great Britain and South Africa. Kenyans began fighting for independence in 1952. By 1963, the country gained its freedom from British rule. ivory cup Ivory comes from elephants and hippos. Many countries today ban the sale of ivory. For a few decades, the president of Kenya had a great deal of power, and the government had only one political party. Many Kenyans wanted to see an end to this inequality. In 2010, a new constitution was passed that gave the president less power and the people more power.
pages.brief: A historical view of Kenya’s past, from early trade with the Middle East and Asia to the trade in enslaved people and ivory. European arrivals, British colonial rule in 1920, and the fight for independence lead to freedom in 1963. An ivory cup appears, and a new constitution in 2010 gives the people more power.

pages.text: On a safari, tourists usually travel in guided vans to search for animals to see and photograph. Animals Kenya is famous for its wildlife, some of which is very rare. To protect its animals, Kenya has set aside more than fifty parks and animal reserves. Every year, millions of tourists go on safari to see animals such as rhinoceroses, lions, leopards, hippos, and elephants. Kenya has two kinds of elephants. The forest elephant lives in the highland rainforests, while the savanna elephant lives in many environments, including deserts. Kenya also has two kinds of rhinoceroses—the white rhino and the black rhino—even though both are actually gray. Rhinos do not see well, but they have keen senses of smell and hearing. Even though they weigh about 3,600 kilograms (8,000 lb.) on average, they can run as fast as 45 kilometers (28 mi.) per hour.
pages.brief: Tourists on safari ride in guided vans, searching for animals to see and photograph. Kenya’s parks and reserves protect rhinoceroses, lions, leopards, hippos, and elephants. Forest elephants live in highland rainforests, while savanna elephants live in many environments. White and black rhinos are both gray, with keen smell and hearing, and can run fast despite their weight.

pages.text: Zebras, gazelles, and other grazing animals fill the Kenyan savanna. One of the most amazing sights in all of Africa is the annual migration of wildebeests and zebras. Every year, about 1.5 million wildebeests and 300,000 zebras migrate over 1,600 kilometers (1,000 mi.) from the Serengeti (ser-en-GEH-tee) Plain to Kenya’s savanna to find food and water. It’s a difficult trip, and every year about 250,000 wildebeests die in the process. Along the way, predators such as lions, leopards, cheetahs, hyenas, and wild dogs follow the herds. One of the most spectacular events is the migratory crossing of the Mara River. Rivers such as the Mara are also home to hippopotamuses. Hippos may look serene and harmless as they move along in the water, but they actually cause more human deaths in Africa than lions. These aggressive, territorial animals stay in the water most of the time, but at night they emerge to feed on grass and other plants. Sometimes they eat crops, which causes conflict between the hippos and people. Hippos’ huge teeth make them very dangerous.
pages.brief: Zebras and gazelles graze across the Kenyan savanna. During the annual migration, about 1.5 million wildebeests and 300,000 zebras travel from the Serengeti Plain, followed by lions, leopards, cheetahs, hyenas, and wild dogs. The Mara River crossing is spectacular. Hippos stay in rivers by day, emerge at night to feed, and defend territory with huge teeth.

pages.text: Other places in Kenya have many animals, too. Thousands, sometimes millions, of greater and lesser flamingos gather on Lake Nakuru in the Great Rift Valley. These wading birds stick their heads into the water to feed on small plants and animals. Flamingos spend most of their time in the water, but another African bird lives only on land. The ostrich is the largest bird in the world, and it lays the largest eggs as well. One egg can weigh 1.35 kilograms (3 lb.). To protect itself from predators, an ostrich may hide by stretching out on the ground. It may also run away, reaching speeds of up to 70 kilometers (43 mi.) per hour. If all else fails, the ostrich can deliver powerful kicks to defend itself. Kenya has several large, dangerous predators, and two that are most harmful to humans are actually very small. The tsetse (TSEE-tsee) fly and the mosquito infest about one-third of the country. These insects carry the diseases of malaria and sleeping sickness. Sleeping sickness gets its name from one of its symptoms: people with the disease become very sleepy. When a tsetse fly or mosquito bites a person, the insect transmits a very small organism that causes disease. Both malaria and sleeping sickness make people very ill.
pages.brief: Thousands of greater and lesser flamingos gather on Lake Nakuru in the Great Rift Valley, feeding in the water. The ostrich, the world’s largest bird, lays the largest eggs, hides flat on the ground, runs fast, and kicks to defend itself. Tsetse flies and mosquitoes infest much of Kenya and spread malaria and sleeping sickness.

pages.text: Nairobi has many government buildings and museums as well as several universities. Conclusion Kenya may be famous for its safaris and savanna, yet the country has much more to offer. The cliffs of the Great Rift tower over a valley filled with life, and many of its animal species cannot be found anywhere else. Kenya’s capital city is the center of industry for the whole country, exporting goods to places all over the world. Kenya is one of the world’s most spectacular nations, filled with an abundance of natural beauty and a multitude of fascinating cultures.
pages.brief: Nairobi shows government buildings, museums, and universities in Kenya’s capital. Beyond the city, the Great Rift cliffs tower over a valley filled with life, and many animal species are found nowhere else. Kenya’s capital is an industrial center that exports goods worldwide, while the country holds natural beauty and many fascinating cultures.

pages.text: Population: 52,573,973 Land: 569,140 sq km (219,746 sq. mi.) Capital City: Nairobi Primary Languages: Swahili, English Primary Religion: Christianity Currency: Kenyan shilling.
pages.brief: A final summary of Kenya shows its population, land area, capital city Nairobi, primary languages Swahili and English, primary religion Christianity, and currency, the Kenyan shilling. Its large population and land size are included with these facts in a quick profile of the nation.

books.title: Brazil
books.art_why: Brazil is a real country today; photographs suit its geography, cities, wildlife and people.

pages.text: Brazil Brazil NORTH AMERICA SOUTH AMERICA Where Is It? Brazil is a country in the eastern part of the continent of South America. It occupies nearly half of the continent and is almost as large as the entire United States. The eastern half of Brazil extends into the Atlantic Ocean. Because Brazil is such a large country, the Atlantic coastline is more than 7,400 kilometers (4,600 mi.) long. That’s almost twice as long as the distance across the entire United States.
pages.brief: A map of South America shows Brazil filling the eastern half of the continent, with the Atlantic Ocean along its long eastern coastline; the country’s great size and its position beside the ocean are clear.

pages.text: The western half of Brazil shares a border with many smaller countries, including Venezuela, Colombia, Peru, Bolivia, Paraguay, Argentina, and Uruguay. In fact, Brazil shares a border with every other South American country except Ecuador and Chile. For many years, the city of Rio de Janeiro (REE-oh DAY zhuh-NAIR-oh), located on the eastern coast, was the capital of Brazil. In the 1950s, Brazilians decided to build a new capital city, Brasília (bruh-ZIL-yuh), near the middle of the country. Construction of the city was a giant undertaking. A huge, wild area had to be cleared, and a network of highways connecting the city with the rest of the country had to be built. A large artificial lake was part of the city plan, and it also had to be dug. Brasília became the official capital of Brazil in 1960. The city was planned to have a population of only a few hundred thousand people. However, by the early twenty-first century, a population of more than two million lived there. This increase in population created some unanticipated problems. The artificial lake became polluted, so a water treatment plant had to be created. In addition, the highway network has begun to threaten natural areas, including the Amazon rainforest.
pages.brief: A map of Brazil shows its long border touching many smaller South American countries, while Brasília sits near the country’s center and Rio de Janeiro lies on the eastern coast; highways and a planned artificial lake are part of the capital’s layout.

pages.text: Like so many countries, Brazil is a melting pot of different ethnic groups. About half of the Brazilian people are of European descent, mainly Portuguese (POR-chuh- geez) but also Spanish, Italian, German, and Polish. In fact, Brazil was a colony of Portugal for three hundred years, and the main language of the country is Portuguese. Others are descendants of people from countries such as Angola and the Congo, who were enslaved and brought to Brazil to work on plantations and in mines. Still other people are descended from the groups of Native peoples who first lived in South America. A large segment of Brazil’s population—about four out of every ten Brazilians—is of mixed ancestry. Of the more than two hundred million people living in Brazil, eight out of ten live in cities, including São Paulo (SOW POW-loh), the largest city in South America. Brazil’s cities have grown rapidly over the past sixty years, and with this rapid growth have come problems. Many people living in poverty have been forced to move onto vacant land at the edge of cities and use whatever materials they can find to build homes. People São Paulo is a large industrial center.
pages.brief: A wide view of São Paulo, a huge industrial city with many buildings stretching to the horizon; people of diverse backgrounds live across Brazil, and some families in poverty build homes from whatever materials they can find at the city’s edge.

pages.text: Some people in Brazil work in banking, construction, education, health care, and other service industries. Along the coast, people may work in the large hotels and restaurants found there. Away from cities, some people work in the mining and oil industries. In addition, farmers grow sugarcane and much of the world’s coffee. This plays an important role in Brazil’s agriculture industry. The agriculture industry also produces oranges and soybeans as well as pork, cattle, chicken, and lumber. Ranching in the southernmost region has a long history. Beginning as early as the 1500s, cowboys called gauchos (GOW- chohz) ran ranches and cared for cattle, sheep, and horses. Over the centuries, gauchos developed their own traditions in clothing, songs, and dances. Modern gauchos still work on ranches in southern Brazil.
pages.brief: A gaucho in traditional clothing stands among cattle, sheep, and horses on a southern Brazilian ranch; elsewhere, workers appear in city service jobs, coastal hotels, mines, oil fields, and farms with sugarcane, coffee, oranges, and soybeans.

pages.text: Brazil’s Landforms Brazil Land Brazil is famous for the Amazon River and Amazon rainforest, both of which lie in the Amazon basin. The Amazon rainforest, the world’s largest tropical rainforest, is known as the “lungs of the planet” because its plants produce about 20 percent of the oxygen for the entire world. Highlands are found in two regions of the country. The highlands of the far north contain mountain ranges, steep cliffs, waterfalls, and deep valleys. The larger highlands in southeast Brazil contain both hills and low mountains.
pages.brief: The Amazon rainforest stretches dense and green beside the wide Amazon River, its plants producing oxygen; in the distance, highlands rise with steep cliffs, waterfalls, and deep valleys, while softer hills and low mountains lie in the southeast.

pages.text: Native to the Pantanal, the capybara is the world’s largest rodent. One of the world’s largest freshwater ecosystems, the Pantanal, is located in central Brazil. It extends for as much as 210,000 square kilometers (81,000 sq. mi.). Waters rise several meters when the rivers flood the land during the wet season (October through March) and then recede. In addition to supporting an amazing variety of life, the Pantanal protects areas downstream from flooding during the wet season. During the dry season, it continuously releases water downstream. The Pantanal also acts as a giant water treatment plant by removing pollutants. In addition, its waterways provide transportation, and the region as a whole plays an important role in Earth’s water cycle. Brazil’s coastal lowlands in the east include beautiful sandy beaches, which are some of the main attractions for tourists visiting the country.
pages.brief: A capybara, the world’s largest rodent, stands in the flooded Pantanal wetlands during the wet season; the water rises around it, and the region supports a great variety of life. Farther east, sandy beaches along Brazil’s coastal lowlands draw tourists.

pages.text: History The earliest known people who lived in Brazil were Native peoples such as the Guarani and Yanomami. Some groups still live in the rainforests and along the banks of the Amazon River. In the early sixteenth century, Portugal conquered the area. At first, the Portuguese used the land to collect a type of wood called pau brasil (POW brah-SEEL), or brazilwood. The Portuguese enslaved Native peoples and forced them to work on huge sugarcane plantations. Later, they enslaved millions of African people and brought them to Brazil to work on coffee plantations and in diamond and gold mines. In fact, more African people were enslaved and transported to Brazil than to the Caribbean and North America combined. In 1822, Brazil became an independent country ruled by Emperor Pedro I. In 1888, slavery in Brazil ended, and in 1889, Pedro II was forced by the military to step down. For the next hundred years, dictators led the country, causing much turmoil and many uprisings. In 1985, the government became a democracy. Today, Brazil faces serious challenges. Poverty and unemployment challenge its people while deforestation threatens the natural environment.
pages.brief: Yanomami people live among rainforest trees near the Amazon River, as their ancestors did; in the background, a plantation and mine recall the enslaved Native and African workers brought by Portugal, while a modern city signals Brazil’s democracy today.

pages.text: In a building called the Sambadrome in Rio, performers sing and dance the samba on elaborate floats during Carnaval. Celebrations Many holidays in Brazil are religious in nature. Most Brazilians belong to the Catholic religion, which was brought to Brazil by the Portuguese. Carnaval, a four-day celebration leading up to Lent, is the largest and most popular holiday in Brazil. During Carnaval, people crowd into Brazil’s streets for parades and dancing. Many people wear elaborate costumes with masks and headdresses. As part of year-long preparations for Carnaval, some Brazilians dance the samba in the samba schools of Rio de Janeiro. The samba was brought to Brazil by enslaved African people many years ago.
pages.brief: Inside the Sambadrome in Rio de Janeiro, performers in elaborate, colorful costumes, masks, and headdresses sing and dance the samba on huge decorated floats during Carnaval, while crowds fill the streets for parades and celebration.

pages.text: Animals Brazil is home to the widest variety of life on Earth. The Amazon rainforest alone includes thousands of different types of insects, fish, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and mammals—from the beautiful to the dangerous. The toucan (TOO-kan) is easy to recognize from its brightly colored bill, which is almost as long as its body. Its plumage includes feathers of black, white, green, yellow, and red. Although toucans are heard all the time, they are rarely seen because they mostly stay high up in the trees. toucan Brightly colored frogs of the Amazon rainforest are lovely to look at, but they are among the most poisonous creatures on Earth. The poison of some species is so deadly that just touching them can kill. The poison in the skin of many of these frogs comes from toxic foods that they eat. In the Amazon River, red-bellied piranhas (pi-RAH-nuhz) hunt in groups of one hundred or more. These meat-eating fish have very sharp teeth and strong jaws. Although they eat animal flesh, they rarely attack humans. Instead, they usually eat dead animals.
pages.brief: A toucan with a brightly colored bill almost as long as its body perches high in the Amazon rainforest trees, its black, white, green, yellow, and red feathers visible; below, brightly colored poisonous frogs sit among leaves, and red-bellied piranhas hunt in the river.

pages.text: The river is also home to a “shocking” snakelike fish called the electric eel. The electric eel can grow to be almost 2 meters (6 ft.) long and weigh as much as almost 22 kilograms (48 lbs.). They deliver a strong electric shock to stun prey and enemies. Other parts of Brazil, such as the Pantanal, also include fascinating animals. Storks and herons build nests in its swamps. Colorful parrots fly overhead. Giant anteaters, jaguars, and deer roam the land. Some animals in the Amazon rainforest and the Pantanal could disappear from Earth forever because of habitat loss. As a result of deforestation, more than one fifth of the Amazon rainforest has been destroyed and is gone forever. Many organizations are working together with the Brazilian government to save these areas.
pages.brief: A long electric eel swims in the Amazon River, capable of delivering a strong shock; above, hyacinth macaws fly and a giant anteater roams the Pantanal, where storks and herons nest in swamps and jaguars and deer move through the land.

pages.text: Futebol Many Brazilians enjoy watching and playing futebol (FOOT-bohl), also known as soccer. Brazil has won the World Cup, the world’s largest soccer tournament, more than any other country. Pelé is the country’s most famous soccer player; he is known around the world. Pelé led the Brazilian team to victory in the World Cup three times—in 1958, 1962, and 1970. Pelé Conclusion Brazil is a colorful mix of different kinds of land, animals, and people.
