pages.text: United Arab Emirates Where Is It? The United Arab Emirates (UAE) is a Middle Eastern country. The Middle East region is located at the hub of three continents: Asia, Africa, and Europe. Most of the countries in the Middle East are entirely in Asia, though some lie either completely or partially in Africa and Europe. The UAE is entirely in Asia. It covers about 83,600 square kilometers (32,278 sq. mi.) of the Arabian Peninsula and shares borders with Saudi Arabia and Oman. The majority of the UAE coastline runs along the Persian Gulf, which is called the Arabian Gulf by people in the region. It flows outward to the Indian Ocean. A small part of its eastern coast lies directly on the Gulf of Oman. In all, the UAE has 1,318 kilometers (819 mi.) of coastline.
pages.brief: The Arabian Peninsula, with the UAE lying between Saudi Arabia and Oman, the Persian Gulf along its northern coast and the Gulf of Oman at its eastern edge; beyond, the wider Middle East connects toward Asia, Africa, and Europe.

pages.text: The UAE is a federation of seven independent Arab states, which include Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah (SHAR-juh), Ajman (ej-MAHN), Umm al Quwain (OOM AHL ky-WAYN), Ras al Khaimah (RAHS AHL KY-muh), and Al Fujairah (AHL foo-JY-ruh). Each state has its own capital city, which shares the name of the state. The federation’s capital city, Abu Dhabi, lies on an island in the gulf. Abu Dhabi, the UAE’s second-largest city, dates back to 3,000 bce. Modern Abu Dhabi blends its ancient culture with contemporary architecture. The city has both stately white-domed mosques and shining skyscrapers. Northeast of Abu Dhabi stands the country’s largest city, Dubai, which serves as a center for trade and tourism. Though both cities show off their wealth, Dubai shines brightly. It is home to the world’s tallest building, the only seven-star hotel, and one of the largest artificial islands. Do You Know? Dubai is one of the fastest-growing cities in the world. In 1968, there were just thirteen cars in the entire city. Today, planners are building double-decker roads for the city’s 1.4 million vehicles. A modern roadway in Dubai.
pages.brief: On an island in the gulf, Abu Dhabi shows white-domed mosques beside shining skyscrapers; northeast, Dubai rises with the world's tallest building, a seven-star hotel, and artificial islands. A modern roadway runs through Dubai, carrying traffic.

pages.text: People Although millions of people live in the UAE, most are not citizens; immigrants make up a majority of the UAE’s total population. Most hail from other Arab countries or South Asia, and have relocated to the UAE for work. The UAE’s citizens, called Emirati, are descended from the Arab tribes that settled the region long ago, and although these tribes have a history of rivalry, many share certain traditions. For example, most UAE citizens prefer to wear traditional Arab clothing. The men wear a long, white, cotton, ankle-length garment, a head covering, and a light scarf (either white or red checkered). Traditional women don two kinds of dress: At home, they might wear a dress with loose pants. Outside, they must dress modestly and usually wear a dark cloak and use a scarf to cover their head. At times women also cover their faces. The scarves have religious meaning but also serve as protection from the sun. A UAE family poses for a portrait. Children wear traditional clothing at more formal occasions.
pages.brief: A UAE family poses for a portrait. The men wear long white ankle-length cotton garments with head coverings and light scarves; the women wear dark cloaks and headscarves, some covering their faces; children wear traditional clothing for a formal occasion.

pages.text: Islam is the most common religion in the UAE, and in 2005, Muslims made up the majority of the UAE population. In the UAE, most people speak Arabic, which is the country’s official language. In schools, students learn Modern Standard Arabic, but most Emiratis also speak dialects of surrounding countries. Many people speak English as well. The UAE’s biggest businesses—oil and construction—are traditionally male-dominated industries, and many of the foreign workers who move to the UAE for jobs are young men without families. Because these foreign workers make up so much of the population, more men than women live in the UAE. Men make up two-thirds of the total population. A construction worker on a skyscraper in Abu Dhabi.
pages.brief: A construction worker stands high on a skyscraper in Abu Dhabi, working on the building far above the ground. The tall structure rises above the city, with the worker balanced on its upper levels as construction continues.

pages.text: Landforms of the United Arab Emirates Almost all of the land in the UAE is desert. Land On the coast, the UAE is hot and humid; swamps and marshes thickly cover the land, while shoals and islands spot the coastline. In the east, the Hajar Mountains rise 2,000 meters (6,500 ft.). Overall, the country receives very little rainfall— the UAE’s yearly rainfall amounts to just 10–15 centimeters (4–6 in.)—but what little it gets falls in the cooler mountain areas. The mountains make up just a small part of the UAE. Inland desert makes up the majority of the UAE’s geography. Here the sun beats down even hotter than on the coast, with desert temperatures that soar as high as 49°C (120°F). Winds from the north sometimes blast the region with dust and sand, which may carry for miles. These winds help create some of the world’s largest sand dunes.
pages.brief: A wide UAE landscape: hot, humid coastal marshes and small islands edge the Persian Gulf; in the east, the rocky Hajar Mountains rise about 2,000 meters. Inland, desert sand stretches under blazing sun, with north winds lifting dust and shaping huge dunes.

pages.text: Although most of the desert is unlivable, oases offer some relief. These desert areas are fertile spots that allow plants and some animals to thrive. The fourth-largest city in UAE is Al Ain, which lies about 160 kilometers (100 mi.) east of Abu Dhabi and has a population of more than 614,000. In the middle of the city is the largest UAE oasis, also called Al Ain, where fruit trees grow. In the desert, plant life is limited to grasses and thorny bushes, but in oases, date palms, alfalfa, mangoes, and other crops are harvested. The UAE’s desert wildlife includes the Arabian oryx, Gordon’s wildcat, sand fox, and sand gazelles. Overhunting has threatened some species, such as the Arabian oryx, with extinction. People came to the oryx’s rescue by taking the animals into captivity and placing them in breeding groups to keep the species going. Arabian Oryx Gordon’s Wildcat Sand Fox Sand Gazelle.
pages.brief: In Al Ain, the UAE's largest oasis, date palms, mangoes, alfalfa, and other fruit trees grow green in the desert. Around the fertile spot, the Arabian oryx, Gordon's wildcat, sand fox, and sand gazelle live; people have taken Arabian oryx into captivity to breed them.

pages.text: History Humans have lived on the Arabian Peninsula for thousands of years. Wandering groups settled in the area and eventually adopted Islam around 600 ce. Over several centuries, the gulf became an important trade route linking Europe to Asia. In the 1600s, England established itself as one of the strongest powers in the region. In the 1700s, the Arab states that make up what we know today as the UAE began to form as sheikhdoms, or areas ruled by leaders called sheikhs, which fought each other for control of the region. Britain took control of trade routes in the region in the early 1800s. In 1820, Great Britain signed a peace treaty, or truce, with the sheikhs of the coastal tribes. Later, these states signed additional truces, and the sheikhdoms came to be called the Trucial States. In the mid-1900s, the Sheikh in control of Abu Dhabi agreed to let British-owned oil companies look over the land. After several decades of searching, the oil company Abu Dhabi Marine Areas detected a large oil deposit in 1958. In the years that followed, oil was also discovered in Dubai and Sharjah, and foreign oil companies quickly began drilling in the Trucial States. The economy of the UAE improved dramatically and quickly.
pages.brief: On the Arabian Peninsula, wandering groups settle and adopt Islam around 600 CE; gulf trade routes link Europe and Asia. Later, Arab sheikhdoms form and fight for control. British oil companies search the land, and in 1958 an oil deposit is detected in Abu Dhabi.

pages.text: Due to financial problems, Great Britain was no longer able to afford to keep a military presence in the region. In 1968, Great Britain announced its plan to withdraw from the gulf. The Trucial States, along with Qatar and Bahrain, decided to form a federation, so they negotiated to decide what the Trucial States would become. Qatar and Bahrain eventually decided to become independent countries, but six of the Trucial States joined together as the UAE in 1971. A seventh state, Ras al Khaimah, joined in 1972. At this point, all the states had gained independence from Britain and became the UAE. The UAE is also a member of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC). Along with Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and Oman, the GCC works together on security and economic projects. For example, the organization has strengthened military cooperation between member countries. Emirati girls carry their country’s flag in a parade on National Day on December 2. Each year, the UAE celebrates its independence on this day.
pages.brief: Emirati girls carry their country's flag in a National Day parade on December 2, celebrating independence. In the background, the seven states of the UAE stand together as a federation; nearby, Gulf Cooperation Council countries cooperate on security and economic projects.

pages.text: Landmarks The Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque in Abu Dhabi is one of the largest and most famous landmarks in the country. The Mosque honors Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al-Nahyan, who helped build the UAE’s strong economy while preserving its Islamic culture. As a building that keeps the traditional domes of Islamic mosque style, the mosque symbolizes Islam’s focus on respect, love, and peace. Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque Emirates Palace Hotel, though not home to royalty, is a landmark of Arab culture. In Abu Dhabi, marked by luxury hotels, the palace stands out. It is located on 85 hectares (210 acres) of landscaped garden space and 1.3 kilometers (0.8 mi.) of private beach property. The palace has 348 luxury rooms, 14 world-class restaurants, and a host of other offerings for visitors to enjoy. At an incredible 830 meters (2,723 ft.), the Burj Khalifa skyscraper in Dubai sets the record as the tallest building in the world. Unlike the Grand Mosque or Emirates Palace, Burj Khalifa is an entirely modern construction, which, for the growing UAE, represents the future of Dubai.
pages.brief: In Abu Dhabi, the Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque stands with traditional domes, honoring Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al-Nahyan. Nearby, the Emirates Palace Hotel rises amid landscaped gardens and private beach. In Dubai, the Burj Khalifa towers as the world's tallest building, a modern symbol.

pages.text: The Burj Khalifa tower took six years to build and opened in 2010. Palm Jumeirah Another record-breaking landmark in Dubai is Palm Jumeirah, one of the world’s largest human-made islands. When viewed from above, the design looks like a palm tree. Originally billed as the eighth wonder of the world, this first-class tourist destination houses four thousand luxury villas and apartments, which some people have made their permanent homes. Parks and ski resorts are tourist spots in most places, but in the desert country of the UAE their mere presence, combined with their enormous size, makes them worthy landmarks. Ferrari World in Abu Dhabi is a huge indoor theme park at 86,000 square meters (925,696 sq. ft.) and the first Ferrari-themed park. Visitors enjoy thrill rides and drive miniature cars. Ski Dubai has slopes, slides, and jumps in its 3,000-square- meter (32,292 sq. ft.) machine-made snow park.
pages.brief: The Burj Khalifa tower, built over six years and opened in 2010, rises over Dubai. Nearby, Palm Jumeirah, a human-made island shaped like a palm tree, holds luxury villas and apartments. Ferrari World in Abu Dhabi offers indoor thrill rides and miniature cars; Ski Dubai has slopes, slides, and jumps on machine-made snow.

pages.text: Conclusion The UAE has a long and interesting history. When oil companies uncovered its vast reserves, the UAE began to flourish economically, and opportunities there drew immigrants. As immigrants continue to move to the UAE, the culture is constantly changing. While it holds onto its Arabic past, modern citizens remain ready to build the UAE bigger and better. The future of the UAE looks bright. Mosques that are hundreds of years old are often surrounded by modern skyscrapers creating a beautiful contrast in the UAE.
pages.brief: Old mosques hundreds of years old stand beside modern skyscrapers in the UAE, showing a striking contrast. People from many countries continue to move there, changing the culture while the country holds onto its Arabic past and looks toward a bright future.

pages.brief: A broad view of the UAE: Abu Dhabi as its capital city, Arabic-speaking Muslim communities, and UAE dirham currency in use. The country covers 83,600 square kilometers and holds a population of 5,927,482 people across its land and coastline.

books.title: Morocco
books.art_why: Modern Morocco, its cities, people, food, animals, and landscapes exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Morocco SPAIN Strait of Gibraltar ATLANTIC OCEAN Rabat ALGERIA MOROCCO Canary Islands (Spain) EUROPE ASIA AFRICA MAURITANIA WESTERN SAHARA Where Is It? Morocco is a country on the coast of northwestern Africa, with shorelines along both the Mediterranean Sea and the Atlantic Ocean. It is slightly smaller than the European country of Spain. In Africa, Morocco’s neighbors are Algeria to the east and southeast, and a territory called Western Sahara along its southern edge. Morocco and Spain are separated by the Strait of Gibraltar, a narrow channel that connects the Mediterranean Sea and the Atlantic Ocean. At the Strait of Gibraltar’s narrowest point, Spain is only about 13 kilometers (8 mi.) away from Morocco.
pages.brief: A broad view of northwestern Africa and nearby Europe, showing Morocco along the Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea, with Algeria to the east and Western Sahara to the south. The Strait of Gibraltar separates Morocco from Spain, with the Canary Islands offshore.

pages.text: The capital of Morocco is Rabat, which is located on the Atlantic coastline at the mouth of the Bou Regreg River, right next to its sister city of Salé. Rabat has a long history stretching back to the twelfth century, and the mix of French and Islamic architecture that exists in the city reflects its past. Rabat is no longer a major port due to a buildup of silt in the mouth of the Bou Regreg River, but for centuries it was a site of much sea traffic—and not all of the activity there was legal. The cities of Rabat and Salé were a hub for pirates from the seventeenth to the nineteenth centuries. They ranged the seas along the coasts of Spain, Italy, England, Ireland, and Iceland. A wall (left) surrounds a section of the Moroccan capital city known as “Old Rabat.”
pages.brief: A view of Rabat, Morocco's capital, on the Atlantic coast at the mouth of the Bou Regreg River beside Salé. A wall surrounds a section known as Old Rabat. The city shows a mix of French and Islamic architecture from its long history.

pages.text: A little more than 33 million people live in Morocco, 60 percent of whom live in urban areas. Casablanca is the largest city, with a population of about 3.5 million. Tourism employs more people than other main industries such as mining and manufacturing. In rural areas, agriculture provides employment for about one-third of Moroccans. With plenty of farmland and a mild climate, Morocco stands out among its neighboring countries for its ability to grow crops. In urban areas, many Moroccan men enjoy getting together in cafés to visit and watch soccer matches on television. Soccer has replaced traditional horsemanship competitions as the most popular sport in Morocco. In large cities, people also enjoy going to see movies, eating in restaurants, shopping in stores or open-air markets, and going to the beach. A musician performs on a street in Rabat. Music is important to Moroccan life. People.
pages.brief: A musician performs on a street in Rabat, with people nearby enjoying city life. In large cities, men gather in cafés to visit and watch soccer on television, while others go to movies, restaurants, markets, or the beach. Casablanca is the largest city.

pages.text: Moroccans are mostly of Berber (native people of the region) descent, Arabic descent, or a mixture of both. There are many young people in Morocco—almost half of the population is under the age of twenty-four. Morocco is a very religious country. Islam is the official religion, and 99 percent of the population is Muslim. Moroccan law consists of both Islamic and secular laws. In 2004, Morocco changed its laws to give women more rights. As a result of these laws, Morocco has one of the highest levels of gender equality among Arab countries. Languages of Morocco People speak Arabic, Berber, and French. Berber Arabic French The sign for the Princess Lalla Meryem School, named after a Moroccan president’s daughter, is in three languages.
pages.brief: People of Berber and Arabic descent, including many young Moroccans, are shown in a religious country where Islam is official. A school entrance for the Princess Lalla Meryem School appears with a multilingual sign. Moroccan law combines Islamic and secular laws, and reforms have given women more rights.

pages.text: Morocco’s Landforms Merja Zerga Rabat Ouzoud Falls ATLANTIC OCEAN Mount Toubkal Land Even with Morocco’s Atlantic and Mediterranean coastlines, much of the land is at an elevation high above sea level. There are two major mountain ranges in Morocco: the Atlas Mountains in the middle of the country, and the Rif Mountains in the north. The tallest mountain in Morocco is Mount Toubkal, which is 4,165 meters (13,665 ft.) high. The mountain ranges receive a lot of rain and snow, which creates a large number of streams. The climate in Morocco varies drastically, from mild Mediterranean temperatures in northern areas and along the coasts to desert conditions in the south. Temperatures in the coastal areas range from 18°C to 28°C (64°F–82°F). Inland areas can be extreme, with temperatures often more than 35˚C (95˚F) in summer and sometimes dropping below freezing in winter.
pages.brief: A landform view of Morocco showing the Atlas Mountains across the middle and the Rif Mountains in the north, the Atlantic coastline, and Mount Toubkal, the tallest peak. Ouzoud Falls and Merja Zerga appear near Rabat, with climate ranging from mild coast to desert south.

pages.text: A hot wind called the sharq ī (shar-KEE) blows out of the Sahara Desert in late spring or early summer. The sharq ī increases the temperatures, often causing heat waves as high as 41˚C (106˚F). The Moroccan landscape is widely varied, ranging from mountains and waterfalls to coastal beaches and desert. In the areas with milder weather, forests cover the land. In some high mountain areas, there are forests of argan trees—a tree that only grows in Morocco. In contrast to the milder areas of Morocco, its Saharan area has few plants except in oases, where people grow date palms. The Sahara Desert in Morocco Ouzoud Falls The Atlas Mountains.
pages.brief: A hot desert wind blows across the Sahara in Morocco, raising temperatures. The varied landscape includes mountains and Ouzoud Falls, coastal beaches, forests of argan trees in high mountain areas, and desert oases where people grow date palms. The Atlas Mountains rise in the background.

pages.text: History More than twelve hundred years ago, Islamic dynasties emerged in what is now Morocco when Idris I, a descendant of the Islamic prophet Muhammad, came to the area from the Middle East. Idris took control from the native people of the region, the Berbers. Later Muslim kingdoms controlled parts of what is today Spain until Catholic rulers forced them out in 1492. After more than a thousand years of independence, Morocco found itself subject to political powers of Europe. Spain established control along the Moroccan coast in 1884. Following civil unrest in Morocco, the rest of the country came under French control in 1912. The French promised to share their military strength and protect the standing of the Moroccan royal house. Morocco was under French rule until 1956. Today, Morocco has both a king and a prime minister. In the 1970s, Spain gave the desert area of Western Sahara to Morocco and Mauritania. Since then, Morocco has fought armed battles with Algeria and Western Saharan groups over this land. The area is a harsh desert, but beneath the barren landscape lie valuable minerals, which could make the country that controls them very rich. Morocco claims and controls most of Western Sahara, but many people still question its claim today.
pages.brief: Idris I arrives from the Middle East and takes control from the Berbers, beginning Islamic dynasties in Morocco. Later Catholic rulers force Muslims out of Spain in 1492. Spain controls the Moroccan coast in 1884, and France rules from 1912 to 1956. Today Morocco has a king and prime minister, with disputes over Western Sahara.

pages.text: Animals Morocco hosts an impressive variety of bird life. Visitors to Merja Zerga (MUR-zhah ZUR- kah), a lagoon on Morocco’s Atlantic coast, can see huge flocks of herons, flamingos, and ducks. The birds are especially numerous in the winter. Northern Africa is home to single-humped camels, or dromedaries, which thrive in Morocco. They play an important part in the country’s tourist industry. Visitors can take a trek through the countryside on a camel. The Barbary macaque (muh-KAK), a forest- dwelling monkey, is another species living in Morocco. Barbary macaques are interesting among macaques because the male monkeys help take care of the young members of their group. Barbary macaques also live across the Strait of Gibraltar in Spain and are the only monkeys living in Europe.
pages.brief: A camel, a flamingo, and a Barbary macaque are shown in Morocco. At Merja Zerga lagoon on the Atlantic coast, large flocks of herons, flamingos, and ducks gather in winter. Single-humped dromedary camels thrive and carry visitors on treks, while Barbary macaques live in forests and male monkeys help care for young.

pages.text: The fennec fox’s large ears help it release body heat to stay cool. Other interesting animals dwell in Morocco’s deserts. For example, fennec foxes, the smallest type of fox in the world, live in the Sahara in Morocco. Fennec foxes are active at night to beat the desert heat. The Moroccan desert is also home to a spider with a very unusual skill. When the spider feels threatened, it flings itself end over end in a manner that is similar to a gymnast’s handspring, or “flic-flac.” The spider can do this flipping move forward or backward, and can even use it to travel uphill. When performing this tricky move, the spider can cover 2 meters (6.6 ft.) per second, twice as fast as it usually travels. The Moroccan flic-flac spider tumbles down a sand dune.
pages.brief: A fennec fox with large ears stands in the Sahara Desert, active at night to beat the heat. Nearby, a Moroccan flic-flac spider flings itself end over end down a sand dune, a flipping move it can use forward, backward, or uphill, covering two meters per second.

pages.text: People from around the world enjoy Moroccan food, which contains elements of Spanish, French, Berber, and Arab cuisines. One of the Moroccan main dishes is couscous, which is a tiny round pasta. As in other Arab countries, people serve bread with meals. Moroccans use a special clay pot called a tagine (tah-ZHEEN) to cook many dishes. The word tagine appears in the names of dishes people cook in this type of pot. Meat is plentiful in Morocco and is featured in dishes such as kebobs of many varieties and a lamb stew that people serve during the holy month of Ramadan. Another popular meat dish is b’stillah (buh-STI-lah), which is a pastry filled with pigeon meat and topped with sugar. People also eat fish regularly in coastal areas. Tomatoes, onions, peppers, and eggplant are hallmark vegetables of Moroccan cuisine. The flavors of garlic, olives, lemons, and spices such as saffron, cumin, coriander, and cinnamon are often present in Moroccan food. People often wash down their meals with mint tea or black coffee. Food chicken tagine.
pages.brief: A Moroccan meal is shown with couscous, bread, and a chicken tagine cooked in a special clay pot. Other dishes include kebobs, lamb stew served during Ramadan, and b'stillah, a pastry filled with pigeon meat and topped with sugar. Tomatoes, onions, peppers, eggplant, garlic, olives, lemons, and spices flavor the food, with mint tea or black coffee.

pages.text: The city of Casablanca shines at night. Conclusion Morocco is a land with an ancient history, filled with snowy mountains, sunbaked desert dunes, and inviting beaches. The different areas are home to a variety of interesting animals. Due to its location, tourists to this unique land find Morocco a bridge to Africa as well as a gateway to Europe. Morocco stands out in the region for its mild climate in the north, its strong ability to grow crops, its reforms regarding gender equality, and its delicious, world-famous cuisine.
pages.brief: The city of Casablanca shines at night, with lights across the city. Morocco is a land of ancient history, snowy mountains, sunbaked desert dunes, and inviting beaches. It is home to a variety of interesting animals and stands out for its mild northern climate, crop-growing ability, gender equality reforms, and world-famous cuisine.

books.title: Mysterious Shipwrecks
books.art_why: Most pages describe historical shipwrecks and events from before photography, so a real photo of the events is impossible.

pages.text: Mysterious Shipwrecks.
pages.brief: A broken wooden shipwreck rests on the seafloor, partially buried in sand and shadowed by deep water. No people or animals are visible. The scene is dark and mysterious, with the wreck's shape hinting at a long-ago sinking. The water is calm and murky, hiding details.

pages.text: Marine Mysteries, Lost and Found The United Nations estimates the world’s coastlines and seafloors are littered with more than three million shipwrecks. Marine archaeologists study some wrecks that date back hundreds, even thousands, of years. Treasure hunters search for other wrecks because of the riches rumored to have sunk with them. In some cases, however, ships have simply disappeared without a trace, leaving no clues that might suggest their fate. A wreck at the bottom of the Red Sea in Jordan Every shipwreck holds some kind of mystery. What was the ship carrying, and where did its wreck end up? What happened to the people on board? The mystery that seizes people’s curiosity the most, however, is this: what really sent the ship to its doom? Stories of shipwrecks are often dramatic tales of danger, death, sunken treasure, and intrigue. Clues can help us solve mysteries, but in most cases, the sea hides the clues to a ship’s fate for years—and sometimes forever.
pages.brief: A sunken shipwreck lies at the bottom of the Red Sea in Jordan. The broken hull is partially buried in sand, surrounded by clear blue water. No people are visible. The wreck is old and mysterious, with scattered debris. The scene is quiet, showing one of millions of shipwrecks that hold secrets.

pages.text: Mystery of Antiquity In 1900, divers found a shipwreck they were not even looking for near the Greek island of Antikythera (an-ti-ki-THEER-uh). The wreck was partially buried under shifting sands 55 meters (180 ft.) beneath the sea’s surface. No one knew how it got there, but Greek archaeologists soon realized the more interesting question was when it got there. The Richest Wreck In 1708, a British warship sent the Spanish galleon San José to the bottom of the sea, along with gold and emeralds intended to fund Spain’s war against Great Britain. For three hundred years, the wreck’s whereabouts remained a mystery— until recently. It was located in 2015 off the coast of Colombia. Ownership of the wreck and its treasures has long been disputed between Spain and Colombia. The goods on-board are estimated to be worth as much as $17 billion, making it one of the most valuable shipwrecks in the world.
pages.brief: On the left, divers explore a shipwreck near the Greek island of Antikythera, partially buried in sand 55 meters deep. On the right, the Spanish galleon San José rests off the coast of Colombia, loaded with gold and emeralds. Both wrecks are old and mysterious, each holding undiscovered secrets.

pages.text: As divers brought artifacts to the surface, researchers began piecing together a historical puzzle. The ship was ancient, more than two thousand years old, and had been loaded with an amazing hoard of art and luxury goods. One of these items has been described as the earliest known computer—a mechanical device that used gears to calculate the precise positions of the stars and planets, possibly for navigation. More than 120 years after the wreck’s discovery, research teams are still diving and studying it.
pages.brief: Divers bring artifacts to the surface from an ancient shipwreck. Researchers examine a mechanical device with gears, described as the earliest known computer, used to calculate star and planet positions. The ship was over two thousand years old and loaded with art and luxury goods. The scene shows the device and the ongoing underwater research.

pages.text: HMS Victory sails through turbulent seas in a painting by Thomas Butterworth. Long Lost Victory HMS Victory was the finest ship in Great Britain’s formidable navy. Launched in 1737, the Victory was armed with 110 cannons, making it the biggest military monster of its time. In early October 1744, the Victory was leading its fleet back to Britain. They were caught in a fierce storm in the English Channel, and the Victory became separated from the other ships. The great warship disappeared along with some 1,150 people. On that fateful night, locals on nearby islands heard the steady booming of cannons—a maritime cry for help. Unfortunately, the seas were far too treacherous for any attempt at rescue.
pages.brief: The HMS Victory, a massive warship with 110 cannons, sails through turbulent seas in a painting. The ship is caught in a fierce storm in the English Channel, separated from its fleet. Dark waves crash around it. The scene is dramatic and dangerous, showing the ship before it disappeared with 1,150 people on board.

pages.text: Artifacts from HMS Victory such as this bronze cannon were discovered by a salvage company. Days later, some wreckage from the vessel washed up on the rocky shores of the islands where the distress signals had been heard. However, the ship’s main body—its hull and decking—was nowhere to be found. It was as though the storm had swallowed it. The disappearance of such a massive ship baffled investigators for more than 250 years. Modern technology helped solve the mystery of the Victory ’s final resting place. In 2008, a marine salvage company searched a wide area using sonar and other advanced equipment. The remains of the ship lay 100 kilometers (62 mi.) from where it was originally believed to have sunk. The salvage company and British government worked together to retrieve valuables from the wreck. Today, the world’s oldest naval ship still in commission bears the name of HMS Victory.
pages.brief: A bronze cannon from HMS Victory is discovered by a salvage company. Wreckage washed up on rocky shores, but the main hull was missing. In 2008, a salvage company using sonar found the ship's remains 100 kilometers from the original believed site. The scene shows the cannon and modern equipment finding the wreck.

pages.text: Ghost Ship: Mary Celeste Not all lost ships end up at the bottom of the sea. Some experience a fate even more mysterious, such as the Mary Celeste ’s. On November 7, 1872, the cargo ship set sail from New York City in the United States, bound for Genoa, Italy. The 30.1-meter (100 ft.) vessel had a crew of seven, plus Captain Benjamin Briggs, his wife, Sarah, and their two-year-old daughter, Sophia.
pages.brief: The Mary Celeste, a 30.1-meter cargo ship, sets sail from New York City harbor on November 7, 1872, bound for Genoa, Italy. On board are Captain Benjamin Briggs, his wife Sarah, their two-year-old daughter Sophia, and a crew of seven. The ship looks normal and seaworthy as it begins its voyage.

pages.text: One month later, the British ship Dei Gratia spotted a vessel drifting in the Atlantic Ocean. It was the Mary Celeste, but a boarding party found no one on the ship. A lifeboat was missing, as was the ship’s navigational equipment, but there were no signs of violence, the crew’s personal gear was stowed, and all the cargo was still in the hold. The last entry in the captain’s log indicated nothing amiss. However, Captain Briggs, his family, and the crew were neither seen nor heard from again. Investigators later examined the Mary Celeste but found few clues about why a seasoned crew would abandon a seaworthy ship. Something, though, seemed to have driven them off the Mary Celeste. The intrigue has led to many fictionalized accounts of the mystery of the Mary Celeste, usually featuring rebel crew members, murder, and even sea monsters. The Fraidy-Cat of Empress of Ireland Emmy was considered the ship’s cat on the Empress of Ireland. The day before the passenger ship sailed from Canada, Emmy fled the vessel. When carried back aboard, she escaped again. Her behavior was viewed as a bad omen. The next day, the Empress of Ireland struck another ship and sank in just fourteen minutes. More than one thousand people died, making it the deadliest wreck in Canadian history.
pages.brief: The Mary Celeste drifts empty in the Atlantic Ocean, spotted by the British ship Dei Gratia. A boarding party finds no one aboard; a lifeboat and navigational equipment are missing. Nearby, the ship's cat Emmy is shown fleeing the Empress of Ireland before that ship sinks after a collision, killing over a thousand people.

pages.text: A painting of HMS Erebus stuck in the ice by François Etienne Musin The Long Hunt for HMS Erebus and HMS Terror In 1845, the British navy mounted the Franklin Expedition to search for the Northwest Passage. It was hoped this new route across the Arctic Ocean would prove a shortcut for shipping between Europe and Asia. Named for its commander, Sir John Franklin, the expedition included 129 people and three years’ worth of supplies on two ships—HMS Terror and HMS Erebus. The pair were designed as sturdy warships but had been refitted to face the fearsome conditions of Arctic exploration. On July 26, 1845, two whaling ships spotted Terror and Erebus in Canada’s Baffin Bay. A year passed with no word from Franklin—then two years. Officials and the public feared for the safety of the explorers. The truth was worse than they imagined.
pages.brief: In a painting, HMS Erebus and HMS Terror are stuck in thick Arctic ice. The two sturdy warships were refitted for exploration. In July 1845, two whaling ships spotted them in Canada's Baffin Bay. The scene shows the ships surrounded by ice, with 129 people and three years of supplies on board, beginning the Franklin Expedition.

pages.text: Search and rescue ships gradually discovered abandoned gear, graves, and notes left by desperate crew members on uninhabited islands. The two ships had been trapped in pack ice in September 1846, and Sir Franklin died the following June. For two years, the sailors—sick and dying—waited in vain for the ice to release their ships. Finally, in April 1848, the survivors attempted a desperate hike southward to reach the Canadian mainland. In 1855, local Inuit told investigators about a group of Europeans who had starved to death along the coast. Evidence showed that the group had resorted to cannibalism to try to survive. The doomed expedition has never ceased to fascinate adventurers. In 2014, a ship equipped with sonar found the wreck of Erebus, well preserved in 12 meters (40 ft.) of frigid Arctic waters. Its partner ship remained missing until September 2016, when the preserved remains of the HMS Terror were found at the bottom of a bay off King William Island. A diver explores the remains of the Erebus.
pages.brief: A diver explores the well-preserved wreck of HMS Erebus in frigid Arctic water. Search ships found abandoned gear, graves, and notes on uninhabited islands. The ships had been trapped in pack ice; survivors attempted a desperate hike south. In 2014, sonar located Erebus, and in 2016, HMS Terror was found off King William Island.

pages.text: Terror on the Rocks: SS Valencia The SS Valencia was one of the most terrifying shipwrecks of all. In January 1906, the passenger steamer was on its way from San Francisco to Seattle with 173 people on board. Near midnight on January 22, its iron hull ran aground near Vancouver Island. Pounding waves trapped the ship, making it nearly impossible for anyone to escape. The crew lowered lifeboats, but most boats flipped, or capsized, in the churning seas, tossing people into freezing water where they drowned. High winds and waves hampered rescue efforts. About thirty-six hours after the stranding, witnesses onshore watched in horror as a huge wave swept over the upper deck, where dozens of passengers were holding on for their lives. In total, only 37 out of 136 passengers survived. A Valencia lifeboat escapes the violent seas, bearing some of the few survivors of the wreck.
pages.brief: The SS Valencia, an iron-hulled passenger steamer, runs aground near Vancouver Island in January 1906. Pounding waves trap the ship as crew lower lifeboats that flip in churning seas. People are tossed into freezing water. A Valencia lifeboat escapes the violent seas, carrying some of the few survivors. The scene is chaotic and terrifying, with rescue hampered by high winds.

pages.text: Valencia leaves San Francisco eight years before the ship’s tragic sinking. How, why, and where were not the mysteries of the Valencia wreck. Investigations concluded the captain and crew had made bad decisions that endangered the ship and its passengers. Most of the mysteries came later and inspired supernatural tales. In 1910, for example, newspapers reported that sailors had seen a ghostly Valencia sailing near the site of the wreck. A rumor also spread that a lifeboat containing eight skeletons had been found in a nearby cave, though the story was never confirmed. Then in 1933—twenty-seven years after the disaster— one of Valencia ’s lifeboats seemed to float out of the past and was discovered in a nearby bay. Its nameplate is now displayed in the Maritime Museum of British Columbia.
pages.brief: The SS Valencia leaves San Francisco harbor eight years before its tragic sinking. Later, a ghostly Valencia is reported sailing near the wreck site. A lifeboat with eight skeletons is rumored to be found in a nearby cave, though never confirmed. In 1933, one of Valencia's lifeboats is discovered in a nearby bay. Its nameplate is displayed in a museum.

pages.text: Gone Without a Trace: USS Cyclops The USS Cyclops was a U.S. Navy supply ship. During World War I, the Cyclops crew picked up a load of heavy ore in Brazil. While there, Captain W. Worley reported to his superiors that one of the engines needed repairs and was not operational. He was told to get it fixed once he reached the United States. On February 22, 1918, the ship left Brazil with a crew of 309. The Cyclops disappeared somewhere in the Atlantic Ocean, and not one piece of wreckage has ever been found. At the time, people speculated that a German submarine had sunk the ship. Some naval officials wondered if Captain Worley, who had been born in Germany, might have secretly handed the ship over to the enemy, though there was no proof of that. The disappearance of USS Cyclops, pictured above, remains the largest loss of life in U.S. naval history in an event not directly related to combat.
pages.brief: The USS Cyclops, a U.S. Navy supply ship, leaves Brazil on February 22, 1918, with a crew of 309. The ship is loaded with heavy ore. Captain W. Worley had reported one engine needing repairs. The Cyclops disappeared somewhere in the Atlantic Ocean, and no wreckage was ever found. The scene shows the ship before it vanished.

pages.text: Some ships have been sunk intentionally in the Bermuda Triangle to create artificial reefs, promoting sea life in the area. Another theory notes the ship disappeared in the Bermuda Triangle, an area in the Atlantic Ocean with a reputation for swallowing ships. Most naval experts think that in addition to lacking full engine power, the ship was overloaded and unstable. They say it may have been caught in a violent storm that occurred on March 10, which could have sent the ship to the ocean floor. The Bermuda Triangle The Bermuda Triangle is an area of the Atlantic Ocean. Its corners are marked approximately by Bermuda, Puerto Rico, and the tip of Florida. According to legend, a high number of unexplained disappearances of ships and aircraft occur there, leading to rumors of supernatural powers sinking or snatching ships. However, researchers have determined that ships are no more likely to disappear there than in other busy shipping areas. pages.brief: A map shows the Bermuda Triangle in the Atlantic Ocean, with corners at Bermuda, Puerto Rico, and the tip of Florida. The USS Cyclops is shown near the triangle. Some ships are sunk intentionally there to create artificial reefs. The map labels the United States, Florida, Bermuda, Caribbean Islands, and Puerto Rico, illustrating the mysterious area.

pages.text: There and Gone: SS Edmund Fitzgerald The SS Edmund Fitzgerald was a huge freighter. On November 9, 1975, the ship left Superior, Wisconsin, fully loaded with iron ore and captained by Ernest McSorley. A storm was forecast, but the veteran captain was not concerned. On the afternoon of November 10, though, the U.S. Coast Guard warned all ships to seek shelter. The Edmund Fitzgerald headed for Whitefish Bay, Wisconsin. At about 7:00 p.m., McSorley reported that the ship was taking on water but radioed, “We are holding our own.”
pages.brief: The SS Edmund Fitzgerald, a freighter loaded with iron ore, leaves Superior, Wisconsin, on November 9, 1975, under Captain Ernest McSorley. A storm is forecast. On November 10, the Coast Guard warns ships to seek shelter. The Fitzgerald heads for Whitefish Bay. At 7:00 p.m., McSorley reports the ship is taking on water but says, 'We are holding our own.'

pages.text: Moments later, the ship was gone. It no longer appeared on radar. No lifeboats were launched. None of the twenty-nine crew members were found. The Coast Guard located the wreck on the lake floor within days. The ship had been snapped in half. Investigators suspect a series of three rogue waves may have sunk the ship so suddenly there was no time even to make a distress call. Rogue Waves Researchers suspect “rogue waves” for some unexplained shipping disasters. What makes these waves so dangerous is their unpredictability, size, and power. A rogue wave comes out of nowhere and is much bigger than the waves around it. It is created by a powerful combination of strong water currents and high winds, usually far out at sea. The sudden jump in wave size can flip large freighters.
pages.brief: The SS Edmund Fitzgerald has snapped in half on the lake floor, located by the Coast Guard within days. No lifeboats were launched, and none of the twenty-nine crew were found. A diagram shows a rogue wave, much bigger than surrounding waves, created by strong currents and high winds. Such a wave may have sunk the ship suddenly.

pages.text: The Slave Wrecks Project Between the 16th and 19th centuries, as many as 1,000 ships carrying enslaved people were lost at sea. Most of those shipwrecks remain undiscovered and undocumented today. Organizations such as the Slave Wrecks Project, founded in 2008, are working to find those lost ships and the historical information they contain. In 2014, the Slave Wrecks Project made its first major recovery—a sunken ship called the São José, located near the coast of Cape Town, South Africa. The Sea Keeps Many Secrets Sailing the seas has always involved an element of danger. The oceans stretch vast distances, weather can turn suddenly treacherous, and threatening reefs and rocks hide along coastlines. Modern equipment makes shipping safer than ever, but dozens of shipwrecks still claim the lives of about two thousand people every year. Working on a ship remains one of the world’s most dangerous jobs. Sailors entrust their lives to their knowledge, skills, and the ships they serve on—but sometimes, their fate is down to luck. Every shipwreck leaves behind mysteries. Some of these mysteries can be explored and eventually explained, and older wrecks may provide us with a glimpse into the past. Much of the time, though, the sea keeps these secrets to itself.
pages.brief: The Slave Wrecks Project works to find lost ships that carried enslaved people between the 16th and 19th centuries. In 2014, the sunken ship São José was recovered near Cape Town, South Africa. The scene shows the underwater wreck. Modern ships sail dangerous seas, where reefs and rocks hide along coastlines. Dozens of shipwrecks claim two thousand lives every year.

pages.text: A fortress on the palace grounds provides stark contrast to Tokyo’s modern skyscrapers. A Green Oasis Tokyo is a sea of towering skyscrapers and glittering lights. However, in the center of this modern city lies a green oasis of manicured gardens and wooden buildings surrounded by traditional stone walls: the Tokyo Imperial Palace. The palace grounds make up one of the most valuable pieces of real estate on Earth. The palace is the home of the emperor and empress of Japan, who belong to the world’s oldest monarchy.
pages.brief: A stone fortress on the palace grounds stands in stark contrast to Tokyo’s modern skyscrapers. In the center of the city, manicured gardens and wooden buildings are surrounded by traditional stone walls; the Tokyo Imperial Palace is shown as a green oasis among skyscrapers and lights, home of the emperor and empress.

pages.text: The Heart of Tokyo The city of Tokyo is located along the Pacific coast of Honshu, the main island of Japan. The Tokyo Imperial Palace is located in the heart of Tokyo, not far from an inlet of Tokyo Bay. It sits near many important cultural sites, such as the Japanese National Theatre, and tourist attractions such as Tokyo Disneyland. Tokyo is home to thirty-five million people. It is the largest metropolitan area in the world. The Imperial Palace is very close to the National Diet Building, where the Japanese parliament meets. Japan’s government is a constitutional monarchy, which means that the emperor shares his power with parliament. The members of parliament make the laws that govern the country, while the emperor holds a more symbolic, ceremonial role.
pages.brief: An overhead view of Tokyo on Honshu’s Pacific coast, with the Imperial Palace in the heart of the city near an inlet of Tokyo Bay. Nearby are the National Theatre, Tokyo Disneyland, and the National Diet Building, where parliament meets, in a city of thirty-five million people.

pages.text: The current palace is located on the site of the former Edo Castle. It is home to Japan’s imperial family. History of the Imperial Palace The site of the present-day Imperial Palace was not always home to Japan’s emperors. For hundreds of years, a series of military leaders called shoguns held most of the power to rule the country, while the emperor held very little. In the early 1600s, a shogun named Tokugawa Ieyasu (ee-e-YAH-soo) began making significant improvements to Edo Castle, which stood where the Imperial Palace is today. The magnificent Edo Castle was the shogun’s home and the largest castle in Japan. Unfortunately, a terrible fire destroyed the main tower in 1657, and the reigning shogun at the time did not have the financial resources to rebuild it. However, the base of that grand tower remains intact on the Imperial Palace grounds even now.
pages.brief: The former Edo Castle site is shown with the present-day Imperial Palace. In the early 1600s, shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu improves the magnificent Edo Castle, the largest in Japan, while a later fire in 1657 destroys its main tower; the stone base still remains on the grounds.

pages.text: The reign of Tokugawa Ieyasu and his heirs lasted more than 260 years. This time in Japan’s history is called the Edo period. In 1868, there was a political revolution that gave the power back to the emperor and ended the reign of the shoguns. After the revolution, the emperor at that time, Emperor Meiji (MAY-jee), decided to relocate the imperial residence from Kyoto, where it had been for almost one thousand years, to the site of the Edo Castle grounds in Tokyo. Emperor Meiji Emperor Meiji ordered that a new palace be built on the site. The construction project faced many challenges, such as earthquakes, budget problems, and destruction from fires. Workers finally finished building the new palace in 1888, twenty years after construction began. The new palace looked like a traditional Japanese building on the outside, but its interior decorations included several Western elements. This was revolutionary because Japan had kept itself relatively isolated from the Western world throughout its past.
pages.brief: Emperor Meiji orders a new palace on the former Edo Castle grounds after the 1868 revolution returns power to the emperor and ends the shoguns’ rule. The construction faces earthquakes, budget problems, and fires, and workers finish the palace in 1888, twenty years after it began. The finished palace looks traditional outside but has Western elements inside.

pages.text: In traditional Japanese society, tables were low and people sat on the ground or in special legless chairs called zaisu (ZY-soo). In the new palace, the emperor requested imported German chairs for Western-style dining tables. In addition, the new palace had Western curtains instead of thin paper screens to cover windows. It also had carpets or French-style wooden floors as well as tatami —straw mats that were the traditional flooring material in Japan. Other deviations from the traditional Japanese style included fireplaces and chandeliers. This palace was home to Japan’s emperors until World War II. During the war, the United States firebombed Tokyo in April of 1942. The United States did not bomb the Imperial Palace directly, but areas next to the palace were hit hard. Fires spread from the surrounding areas to the palace grounds and significantly damaged the main palace building. The new Imperial Palace dining room (left) included Western-style tables and chairs instead of the traditional Japanese style (right).
pages.brief: Inside the new palace, the emperor’s Western-style dining room has imported German chairs and tables, Western curtains, carpets or French wooden floors, fireplaces, and chandeliers, contrasting with traditional tatami and low seating. During World War II, fires from firebombed areas next to the palace spread onto the grounds and significantly damaged the main palace building.

pages.text: After World War II, Japan rebuilt the palace, completing reconstruction in 1968. Workers built the new palace using modern building techniques and supplies, but they were able to maintain its historical appearance. As a result of this history, some structures on the Imperial Palace grounds, such as the palace itself, are only a few decades old, while others have been there for centuries. For example, the stone base of the old Edo Castle main tower and some sections of the stone walls surrounding the castles are from the Edo period. Some of the wooden guard houses and bridges from the Edo period have also survived. The Imperial Household Agency The Imperial Household Agency building was built on the Tokyo Imperial Palace grounds in 1935. The royal family lived there temporarily after World War II while the new palace was being constructed.
pages.brief: After World War II, workers rebuild the palace by 1968 with modern techniques while keeping its historical appearance. On the grounds, the stone base of the old Edo Castle main tower, some stone wall sections, wooden guard houses, and bridges survive from the Edo period, and the Imperial Household Agency building stands nearby.

pages.text: Construction of the Palace Workers built the original stone walls that surround the palace grounds during the Edo period. They used a centuries-old construction method called kirikomihagi (kee-ree-koh-mee- HAH-gee). This construction technique started by forming the earth into a narrow stairlike shape. Next, builders arranged a layer of small rocks to allow for rainwater drainage. After preparing the ground, workers began to stack the stones to form the walls. The workers did not use mortar to glue the stones together—despite having the technology to do so—because leaving empty cracks between the stones allowed rain to drain out of the walls. If the water couldn’t drain out, the walls would have been damaged by Japan’s heavy rains. Japan also has many earthquakes, and the mortarless building technique made the walls better able to withstand them. The workers built the walls with a slight incline. The slope made the walls easier for enemies to climb but also made them more earthquake proof. The walls at the Otemon Gate were constructed using the kirikomihagi method in the Edo period.
pages.brief: Workers build the palace’s stone walls during the Edo period using the kirikomihagi method: they shape the earth, add small rocks for drainage, and stack stones without mortar. The cracks let heavy rain drain out and help the walls withstand earthquakes. The walls have a slight incline, as seen at the Otemon Gate.

pages.text: Traditionally, Japanese buildings were made of wood, like the Suwano-chaya (su-WAH-noh-CHAH-yah) Tea House on the palace grounds. When Emperor Meiji built his palace, he considered using stone. There was even an attempt to build a stone dining hall on the premises, but this project was abandoned after an earthquake caused the structure to crack. This incident served as evidence that wooden buildings were more reliable in a land of frequent earthquakes. Emperor Meiji decided to build his palace out of wood, in the traditional Japanese style. After World War II, workers used steel- reinforced concrete instead of wood to rebuild the Imperial Palace. However, the palace still has the look of traditional Japanese architecture, especially the sloping roof with long eaves.
pages.brief: The Suwano-chaya Tea House shows traditional wooden Japanese building style on the palace grounds. Emperor Meiji considers stone but abandons a stone dining hall after an earthquake cracks it, so he builds his palace from wood. After World War II, workers rebuild with steel-reinforced concrete while keeping a traditional sloping roof and long eaves.

pages.brief: An overview of the Imperial Palace grounds shows the Outer Garden, East Gardens, Kitanomaru Park, Nijubashi Bridge, and several museums, including the Science Museum, Tokyo National Museum of Modern Art, and Museum of Imperial Collections. The grounds are surrounded by moats and defensive stone walls, some from the Edo period.

pages.text: Nijubashi Bridge The Palace Grounds The palace grounds are divided into four sections: the Imperial Palace Outer Garden, the Imperial Palace inner grounds, Kitanomaru Park, and the East Gardens. The Imperial Palace Outer Garden is a public park. It has large grassy areas and groves of trees that provide a variety of beautiful scenery with each season. The famous Nijubashi Bridge connects the Outer Garden with the Imperial Palace inner grounds. The view of the bridge stretching over the moat with a guard tower in the background is very popular with tourists and photographers. Nijubashi Bridge is opened only for special occasions, such as when important guests attend events at the palace. It is open to the public twice a year—once on January 2 so the people and the emperor can exchange New Year’s greetings, and once to celebrate the emperor’s birthday.
pages.brief: Nijubashi Bridge stretches over the moat, connecting the Imperial Palace Outer Garden with the inner grounds; a guard tower stands in the background. The public park has large grassy areas and groves of trees that change with the seasons, while the bridge opens for special occasions and twice a year for New Year greetings and the emperor’s birthday.

pages.text: The Imperial Palace itself contains 24,175 square meters (about 260,000 sq. ft.) of space, which is about the size of four and a half soccer fields. It is two stories high with an additional level belowground. The palace has rooms for the emperor’s state business, audience rooms, a dining room, a banquet hall, and drawing rooms where guests can relax. The rooms of the palace surround an open courtyard in the center. The emperor uses the palace for ceremonies to appoint prime ministers, Supreme Court justices, and ambassadors. The emperor also meets representatives of foreign governments at the palace and treats them to elegant state dinners. When the emperor and empress greet the public twice a year, they do so from a palace balcony. Emperor Akihito and Empress Michiko greet New Year’s visitors to the Imperial Palace in January 2017.
pages.brief: The two-story Imperial Palace contains rooms for state business, audiences, dining, banquets, and drawing rooms around an open central courtyard. Emperor Akihito and Empress Michiko stand on a palace balcony to greet New Year’s visitors in January 2017, while the emperor also uses the palace for ceremonies, meetings with foreign representatives, and elegant state dinners.

pages.text: Near the palace lies the building of the Imperial Household Agency, which oversees the imperial family’s schedules and events and maintains the palace grounds. This section of the site is also home to the Imperial Cocoonery, where empresses of Japan have been raising silkworms since 1871. The silk from the empress’s silkworms is used to repair ancient kimonos. The residence of the emperor and empress as well as private Shinto shrines for the imperial family are in this area of the palace grounds, too. Empress Michiko attaches silkworm eggs to an oak twig in the Imperial Cocoonery. Kitanomaru Park, in the northern part of the site, became a public park in 1969. Kitanomaru Park offers visitors lovely scenery, especially in spring when the cherry trees are in bloom. The park is home to the Science Museum and National Museum of Modern Art. These attractions offer an interesting contrast between historic sites from the Edo period and the modern exhibits displayed in the site’s museums.
pages.brief: Near the palace, the Imperial Household Agency oversees the imperial family’s schedules and the grounds. Empress Michiko attaches silkworm eggs to an oak twig in the Imperial Cocoonery, where empresses have raised silkworms since 1871. Kitanomaru Park, a public park since 1969, has spring cherry trees and is home to the Science Museum and National Museum of Modern Art.

pages.text: A scroll painting (main) from the early seventeenth century shows Edo Castle; the stone foundation (inset) of Edo Castle’s original main tower still stands today. The East Gardens are another free public park. They feature picturesque ponds, lawns, and many different trees, shrubs, and flowers. This area is also home to Japan’s last garden from the Edo period. In addition to the beautiful scenery, the East Gardens have many interesting historical sites, such as guard houses, walls, and gates from the Edo period. The stone foundation of the former Edo Castle is located in the East Gardens. The gardens also have the Museum of Imperial Collections, where visitors can see portions of the imperial family’s art collection. This art has been passed down from one generation of the imperial family to the next for many years, and it includes masterpieces from as far back as the fourth century.
pages.brief: A scroll painting from the early seventeenth century shows Edo Castle, while the stone foundation of its original main tower still stands today. The East Gardens are a free public park with ponds, lawns, trees, shrubs, flowers, guard houses, walls, gates, and the Museum of Imperial Collections.

pages.text: The Imperial Palace Today The Tokyo Imperial Palace plays a very important role in modern-day Japan. The emperor performs many of his state duties, such as receiving foreign officials and awarding honors, at the Imperial Palace. In addition to its governmental importance, the Imperial Palace is a popular site for tourists and Tokyo residents alike. Many joggers enjoy running a route around the palace grounds, and the palace offers a quiet spot for reflection in the midst of fast-paced city life. A Nature Sanctuary Emperor Hirohito (reigned 1926–1989) was a dedicated nature lover. He did not allow his gardeners to use pesticides and preferred that the gardens be inviting to insects. As a result of his approach, the Imperial Palace grounds are home to more than 3,600 animal and insect species, 1,366 plant species, and 20 percent of Tokyo’s trees.
pages.brief: The Tokyo Imperial Palace plays an important role in modern Japan, where the emperor receives foreign officials and awards honors. Joggers run a route around the grounds, and the palace offers a quiet place for reflection in the city. Emperor Hirohito’s pesticide-free gardens make the grounds a nature sanctuary with thousands of animal, insect, and plant species.

pages.text: In the springtime, over 260 cherry trees burst into bloom, their delicate pink flowers stretching over the Chidori-ga-fuchi moat in the northwest area of the Imperial Palace grounds. This area is the most popular location for cherry blossom viewing in Tokyo. Over a million people visit the moat from late March to early April each year. Visitors can enjoy walking on a footpath beneath a canopy of cherry blossoms or marvel at the beauty while gliding along the waters in a rowboat. An important historic, cultural, and governmental site such as the Imperial Palace must be very carefully maintained. The Imperial Household Agency is in charge of running the palace grounds. The agency has about one thousand employees devoted to these tasks. It spends billions of yen (millions of U.S. dollars) each year; in 2016, the agency spent about 5.5 billion yen ($48 million U.S.) on palace expenses. Cherry trees bloom in spring along the Chidori-ga-fuchi moat.
pages.brief: In spring, more than 260 cherry trees bloom with delicate pink flowers over the Chidori-ga-fuchi moat in the northwest area of the Imperial Palace grounds. Visitors walk on a footpath beneath the blossoms or glide along the water in a rowboat, while the Imperial Household Agency maintains the grounds with about one thousand employees.

pages.text: The Imperial Palace is in the center of Tokyo. The city of Tokyo expanded outward from the palace. A Site of Tranquility The Imperial Palace seems to be a place untouched by time. In the heart of bustling Tokyo, its lush grounds contain thick, impenetrable forests. Its serene gardens and graceful wooden buildings are a balm for weary souls. The palace grounds have been home to shoguns and emperors for centuries. As a cherished part of Japanese history and culture, they will no doubt be a beloved part of Tokyo life for generations to come.
pages.brief: The Imperial Palace sits in the center of Tokyo, and the city expanded outward from it. Its lush grounds contain thick, impenetrable forests, serene gardens, and graceful wooden buildings that feel untouched by time, a balm for weary souls in bustling Tokyo. For centuries the grounds have been home to shoguns and emperors.
