pages.text: Water Cities.
pages.brief: A wide view of a waterside city with buildings beside canals and boats resting on the water, opening the book’s look at places built on or near water around the world. The scene suggests many kinds of water cities without naming a single place.

pages.text: Boats traverse the Grand Canal, the main waterway in the city of Venice, Italy, transporting people and goods between the many islands on which the city was constructed. Living Near Water People from across the globe flock to Venice, Italy, to see the famous city of canals and bridges built on more than a hundred islands. Although Venice is the world’s best-known water city, it is by no means the only one. Water cities are places that are built on or near a body of water. They range from tiny communities to huge urban areas and are located alongside—or in—oceans, seas, bays, lakes, and rivers on every continent in the world except Antarctica. They exist for many reasons, and each one has a fascinating story to tell.
pages.brief: Boats travel along Venice’s Grand Canal, carrying people and goods between the many islands on which the city was built. The scene opens outward to other water cities, from tiny communities to huge urban areas, beside or within oceans, seas, bays, lakes, and rivers on every continent except Antarctica.

pages.text: Europe Amsterdam, Netherlands Amsterdam is another European city famous for its canals. It is the capital and largest city in the Netherlands, a country with roughly one-third of its land below sea level. About 17 percent of the country is built on polders—large areas of land that people have reclaimed from lakes and the North Sea by pumping out water. Amsterdam itself is about 2 meters (6.6 ft.) below sea level. The city was founded in the late twelfth century as a fishing village and became an important seaport in the seventeenth century. It is now one of Europe’s largest seaports.
pages.brief: Amsterdam, Netherlands, shows canals lined with buildings. The city sits about two meters below sea level, in a country where one-third of the land is below sea level. Nearby polders are areas reclaimed from lakes and the North Sea by pumping out water. Amsterdam began as a late twelfth-century fishing village and became an important seaport in the seventeenth century.

pages.text: Amsterdam was encircled by a moat from 1480 to 1585. Its population surged in the 1600s as the city grew. Workers drained swampland and built three more concentric half-circle canals around the downtown area. The four waterways were used for transportation, defense, and water management. Besides the main canals, about 160 others, totaling over 100 kilometers (62 mi.) in length, divide Amsterdam into close to 100 small islands joined by over 1,200 bridges. Although the canals were the city’s main transportation routes for centuries, they are now mainly used by smaller barges and boats. However, they continue to play a key role in the city’s distinctive character. Reine, Norway A tiny Norwegian fishing village more than 100 kilometers (62 mi.) above the Arctic Circle has earned the nickname “The Most Beautiful Place in the World.” Located along the coast of one of the Lofoten Islands, Reine offers fishing, kayaking, skiing, whale watching, hiking, and gorgeous beaches. It’s also a perfect place for dramatic views of the northern lights.
pages.brief: A drawing of Amsterdam shows concentric half-circle canals around the downtown, with barges on the waterways and bridges joining many small islands. In Reine, Norway, a tiny fishing village on a Lofoten Island lies above the Arctic Circle, beside beaches and mountains, with northern lights above.

pages.text: Singapore, the world’s only island city-state, is not just one of the busiest port cities in Asia; it is one of the busiest port cities in the whole world. Asia Singapore Singapore is the world’s only island city-state— an island that is both a city and an independent country. It is composed of sixty-three islands. The country has few natural resources, so it must import almost everything. Projects begun in the 1960s have increased Singapore’s land area by almost 25 percent. Unlike Amsterdam, which has reclaimed land by removing seawater, Singapore has extended its coastline by dumping rocks and sand into the water. A project launched in 2016 will pump out water to create polders, as in Amsterdam. Urbanization over the years has prompted the government to plant greenery and turn Singapore into a city in a garden. Close to one-tenth of its land is now parks and nature reserves.
pages.brief: Singapore appears as a busy island city-state and port, with ships around its coast. Its land area has grown through projects since the 1960s; rocks and sand are dumped into the water to extend the coastline. Greenery is planted across the city, and close to one-tenth of the land is parks and nature reserves.

pages.text: Dubai, United Arab Emirates Dubai is the capital of one of seven political territories in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The country became wealthy due to the discovery of oil in the 1960s. Its economy is now focused on tourism, real estate, and other industries. Dubai is the site of many construction projects, including Palm Islands—three artificial islands shaped like palm trees. The islands are being built along the coast by piling up enormous amounts of sand and rock. They are adding hundreds of miles of coastline to the city as well as residences for many thousands of people. Construction began in 2001; the first one was completed in late 2016. A crescent-shaped breakwater around the island protects it from strong waves and storms. Palm Jumeirah, in the country of Dubai, is part of the Palm Islands development on the Persian Gulf and is one of the largest artificial islands in the world. It was designed to resemble a palm tree when seen from above.
pages.brief: Dubai, United Arab Emirates, shows the Palm Islands being built along the Persian Gulf coast by piling up sand and rock. Palm Jumeirah is shaped like a palm tree when seen from above, with a crescent-shaped breakwater around it. Construction began in 2001, and the first island was completed in late 2016.

pages.text: Africa Ganvié, Benin In startling contrast to the modernity of Singapore and Dubai is Ganvié (GAWN-vye), the largest stilt village in Africa. The village is located in the middle of Lake Nokoué (NOHK-we) in the country of Benin. Ganvié has about twenty thousand residents and three thousand buildings. Only the school and a partially built cemetery are located on land. Ganvié had its origins in the seventeenth- century West African slave trade. During that period, a powerful tribe named the Fon captured and sold people from other tribes into slavery. The Fons’ religion prohibited them from pursuing people who lived on water.
pages.brief: Ganvié, Benin, is a large stilt village in the middle of Lake Nokoué, with about twenty thousand residents and three thousand buildings above the water. Only the school and a partially built cemetery stand on land. Its origins lie in the seventeenth-century West African slave trade, when the Fon people would not pursue those who lived on water.

pages.text: Another tribe, the Tofinu, fled to Lake Nokoué to avoid capture. They founded the stilt village and established a way of life that thrives to this day. Their success is reflected in the name of their village, which means “we survived.” Villagers rely in large part on fishing for their livelihood. They contain and breed fish using a network of underwater fences. They also keep chickens and goats on patches of grass that grow in the water. People travel in long, narrow canoes called pirogues. Fadiouth (Shell Island), Senegal The residents of Fadiouth (fad-YOOT), Senegal, live on an island made up entirely of clamshells. For over three centuries, they have been eating clams and recycling the shells to make not only buildings and streets but also the land itself. The shells are held in place by the roots of trees and reeds.
pages.brief: Tofinu villagers in Ganvié travel in long, narrow pirogues and fish with underwater fences; chickens and goats stand on patches of grass in the water. At Fadiouth, Senegal, residents live on an island made entirely of clamshells, where shells form buildings, streets, and land held in place by tree roots and reeds.

pages.text: The Uru people, the inhabitants of the Uros Floating Village in Lake Titicaca, Peru, craft canoes out of reeds that grow on the lake shore and utilize them for transportation. South America Uros Floating Village, Peru Like the Tofinu, the residents of Uros, a floating village in Peru, moved to water for safety. The Uru people fled to Lake Titicaca over five hundred years ago when the Inca and Colla peoples took over their land. Approximately two thousand Uru now live on about seventy floating islands made of totora reeds. The islands, which are 1.2 to 2.4 meters (4–8 ft.) thick, disintegrate from the bottom. New reeds are continually added to the top. The Uru people also use the reeds to make canoes, homes, and furniture. They make their living from fishing and selling handicrafts. Though the Uru maintain old traditions, they enjoy some modern amenities. The community has a radio station, and some residents have solar panels and motorboats.
pages.brief: In Lake Titicaca, Peru, the Uru people live on about seventy floating islands made of totora reeds. They craft canoes, homes, and furniture from reeds and travel by reed canoe. The islands are thick layers of reeds that disintegrate from the bottom as new reeds are added on top. Some homes have solar panels, motorboats, and a community radio station.

pages.text: Mexcaltitán rests on an isolated bar of sand 400 meters (1,300 ft.) long off the Pacific coast of Mexico. North America Mexcaltitán, Mexico The Aztec people ruled large areas of Mesoamerica between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries. According to legend, they came from Aztlán (ahst-LAHN), a mythical island in a lagoon, which might have been a real place located in northern Mexico. Then their gods instructed them to seek out a new homeland. After a pilgrimage of two hundred years, they founded Tenochtitlán, their capital city. After the Spanish conquest in 1521, Tenochtitlán became known as Mexico City.
pages.brief: Mexcaltitán, Mexico, rests on an isolated sandbar about four hundred meters long off the Pacific coast. The scene recalls the Aztec legend: the Aztec people came from Aztlán, a mythical island in a lagoon that may have been a real place in northern Mexico. After a two-hundred-year pilgrimage, they founded Tenochtitlán, which became Mexico City after the Spanish conquest in 1521.

pages.text: Some historians think that Mexcaltitán (mes-kahl-tee-TAHN), a small human-made island near the Pacific coast of Mexico, is where the Aztec civilization had its beginnings. Ancient manuscripts show that the early Aztecs traveled by canoes similar to those used by the inhabitants of Mexcaltitán. Furthermore, a map from 1579 shows Aztlán and Mexcaltitán to be in exactly the same place. Mexcaltitán, which is about 350 meters (1,150 ft.) by 40 meters (130 ft.), is now home to about eight hundred people. They live in tile-roofed houses made of adobe, brick, and cement. Many make their living by catching shrimp for local restaurants. This water town is sometimes called the Mexican Venice. In summer during the rainy season, boats are the only way to travel through the streets. The local children have fun playing “water soccer” on the island’s only soccer pitch, which is underwater. The inhabitants of Mexcaltitán, Mexico travel by boat and swim in the streets during the flood season on the island.
pages.brief: Mexcaltitán, a small human-made island off Mexico’s Pacific coast, has about eight hundred people in tile-roofed adobe, brick, and cement houses. Many catch shrimp for local restaurants. In the rainy season, boats are the only way through the streets, and children play water soccer on the island’s only soccer pitch, which is underwater.

pages.text: Auckland might not be the capital of New Zealand, but it is that country’s largest city. Oceania Auckland, New Zealand This modern city of 1.5 million people is on the North Island of New Zealand in the South Pacific Ocean. Auckland is located between two large harbors on an isthmus less than 2 kilometers (1.2 mi.) wide at its narrowest point. The harbors open to the Pacific Ocean to the east and the Tasman Sea to the west. Auckland’s nickname is the “City of Sails.” About one-sixth of Aucklanders own a boat, and the city has hosted the America’s Cup yacht race twice. Residents and visitors alike enjoy the thousands of beaches. Water-related activities include kayaking, parasailing, swimming, surfing, boating, fishing, diving, and beach horseback riding.
pages.brief: Auckland, New Zealand, is a modern city of 1.5 million people on the North Island in the South Pacific Ocean. It lies between two large harbors on a narrow isthmus, with the Pacific Ocean to the east and the Tasman Sea to the west. About one-sixth of Aucklanders own a boat, and people enjoy beaches and water activities.

pages.text: California Italy Aircraft carrier People and Water Many kinds of water cities exist besides the ones you’ve just read about. For instance, there’s a tiny Italian fishing town made up of a jumble of brightly colored homes that cling to steep, rocky cliffs. A floating community located in Northern California has fancy, simple, and vintage houseboats. Aircraft carriers—huge seagoing ships designed to launch aircraft—house thousands of people in the military for months at a time. Water represents different things to different people. For residents of water cities, it may mean recreation, a link to nature, or a way of life. It may also mean safety, survival, or an essential connection with the rest of the world. The remarkable diversity of water cities around the world is a testament to human adaptability and innovation.
pages.brief: A tiny Italian fishing town shows brightly colored homes clinging to steep, rocky cliffs. In Northern California, a floating community has fancy, simple, and vintage houseboats. A huge aircraft carrier at sea carries aircraft and houses thousands of military people for months. Together these scenes show water cities as places of recreation, safety, survival, and connection with the world.

books.title: John Muir
books.art_why: John Muir is a named historical person, so the biography rule calls for cartoon art.

pages.text: A Passion for Nature Long ago, when settlers began colonizing what is now the western United States, many spoke about conquering nature. While Indigenous peoples in the area had managed and protected the land for thousands of years, the settlers wanted to clear the land and use natural resources without restraint. John Muir explored nature as a way of becoming closer to what he considered “the heart of the world.” John Muir was one of the few settlers who wanted to preserve nature. His passion for the natural world lured him away from crowded places to live for years in remote cabins. It drew him to explore—on foot—vast areas of California as well as travel to many other parts of the world. Muir’s ideal of a pristine, untouched “wilderness” influenced his ideas about nature. He was an avid supporter of environmental protection, so much so that he supported setting aside land to establish national parks. John Muir was also an eloquent writer and speaker. He used these skills to inspire others to become involved in the conservation movement, which could be harmful to Indigenous peoples.
pages.brief: Settlers clear land and take natural resources without restraint while Indigenous people tend and protect the same land; John Muir walks alone through remote California woods, looking toward mountains and trees as he seeks what he calls the heart of the world.

pages.text: John Muir’s birthplace in Scotland is now a museum dedicated to his life and work. Early Life John Muir was born on April 21, 1838, in Dunbar, Scotland. His father, Daniel, was a businessman and former soldier. His mother, Anne, was a homemaker, painter, poet, and nature lover. John was the oldest son in a family with eight children. In 1849, when John was eleven, the family moved to Wisconsin, in the United States, so Daniel could start a farm and earn more money. Daniel was a strict disciplinarian who forced John and his siblings to work long hours doing farm labor and allowed them only one small meal a day. The children’s health suffered as a result.
pages.brief: The birthplace building of John Muir in Dunbar, Scotland, now a museum dedicated to his life and work; young John stands with his parents and seven siblings at a Wisconsin farm, where his strict father makes the children work long hours with little food.

pages.text: John received no formal education during those years, yet he had a deep thirst for knowledge. John rose at 1:00 a.m. each morning, thrilled to have five extra hours each day to pursue his interests. He studied literature, philosophy, mathematics, and geometry on his own. Any free daylight hours were spent exploring the woods and fields around the family farm. During John’s teen years, he became an accomplished inventor. He spent some of his early-morning time on his inventions, which included water wheels and weather instruments. A later invention—a makeshift “alarm clock”—pushed him out of bed at a designated time. John Muir’s “alarm clock” was a combination desk and clock that attached to a collapsing bed. At the appointed time, the invention lit a lamp and gently deposited John on the floor.
pages.brief: At one in the morning, young John Muir studies literature, philosophy, mathematics and geometry by lamplight; beside him are his water wheel, weather instruments, and a desk-clock alarm bed that lights a lamp and tips him onto the floor.

pages.text: Freedom and Connecting to Nature As a young adult, Muir was restless to follow his passions and escape from the farm. When he was twenty-two, a neighbor suggested that Muir show his inventions at the 1860 Wisconsin State Agriculture Fair in Madison. The inventions, particularly Muir’s “alarm clock,” were a huge hit. Jeanne Carr, one of the judges and Muir’s future mentor, awarded him a cash prize. For the first time in his life, Muir had some independence. Instead of returning home, he decided to stay in Madison and attend college. Jeanne Carr, a writer and amateur botanist, and Ezra Carr, a geology professor, became friends and teachers of Muir’s.
pages.brief: At the 1860 Wisconsin State Agriculture Fair in Madison, twenty-two-year-old John Muir displays his inventions, especially his alarm-clock bed, to judges; Jeanne Carr, a writer and botanist, awards him a cash prize while Ezra Carr, a geology professor, looks on.

pages.text: In the fall of 1860, Muir was flourishing in his new life. He was studying botany—the science of plants—which, as he later wrote, “sent [him] flying to the woods and meadows in wild enthusiasm.” Though Muir also studied geology and chemistry, he did not complete a degree program. A young John Muir In 1863, he left Madison to attend what he called the “University of the Wilderness.” He traveled on foot around Canada and parts of the northern Midwest, closely observing nature and taking odd jobs to pay his way. In 1866, Muir took a job working as a mechanic in Indianapolis, Indiana. The following year, he suffered a work-related eye injury that temporarily blinded him. Although he feared that he would permanently lose his vision, it returned over a period of a month. Able to see again, Muir suddenly realized that his interest in inventions kept him from what he loved most. He left his job and vowed to spend the rest of his life in nature.
pages.brief: A young John Muir studies plants in a meadow near Madison, then stands in an Indianapolis workshop with his eyes bandaged after a work injury; when his sight returns, he leaves machines behind and vows to spend his life in nature.

pages.text: Muir took off on September 1, 1867, hiking about 1,000 miles (1,609 km) to Florida along the “wildest, leafiest, and least trodden way,” he recalled in his writings. He covered at least 20 miles (32 km) a day and took detailed botanical notes during the trip. Muir reached the Gulf Coast in just over seven weeks but fell seriously ill just days later. He had contracted malaria while crossing Florida’s swampland. Muir’s 1867 Trip to Florida Indianapolis by train by foot Ohio by boat West Virginia Indiana Kentucky The following January, partially recovered but still in poor health, Muir boarded a ship to Cuba. He hoped to eventually travel to the Amazon to study the native plants but instead went to San Francisco. Arriving on March 28, 1868, he asked someone to show him the closest way out of town. When the man asked where he wanted to go, Muir replied, “To any place that is wild.” Virginia Tennessee North Carolina South Carolina Alabama Georgia ATLANTIC OCEAN Florida Cedar Keys.
pages.brief: John Muir hikes alone through woods and swampland from Indiana toward Florida, taking botanical notes each day; later, weak from malaria, he boards a ship, then arrives in San Francisco and asks a man for the closest way out of town.

pages.text: Sierra Nevada Region The High Sierra Traveling on foot, Muir headed for California’s Sierra Nevada. The natural beauty of the area filled him with awe. Although Muir was lonely without human connection, he was ecstatic to be in the woods and fields. When he faced a choice between people and nature, the call of nature generally won out. California San Francisco Ahwahnee (Yosemite) Valley PACIFIC OCEAN Muir’s first trip to the High Sierra was short, but he returned the following year. He worked briefly as a shepherd and then took a job running a sawmill near Yosemite (yoh-SEH-muh-tee) Falls. Muir spent his free time exploring the land and celebrating nature. He drew inspiration from the writings of Ralph Waldo Emerson, a famous writer and lecturer who often wrote about the importance of connecting with nature. Ralph Waldo Emerson.
pages.brief: John Muir walks into California's Sierra Nevada and Yosemite Valley, filled with awe at the woods and fields; he works as a shepherd and sawmill operator near Yosemite Falls and draws inspiration from Ralph Waldo Emerson's writing about connecting with nature.

pages.text: In the early 1870s, Muir proposed a controversial theory that the movement of glaciers had carved Yosemite Valley. Muir’s fascination with glaciers led him deep into the mountains to search for evidence. In October of 1871, he wrote an article about glaciers that was printed in the New York Tribune. His theory was confirmed over time. People were beginning to take notice of Muir and his nature observations. Other naturalists went out to his cabin in Yosemite to meet with him, including Emerson in 1871. Do You Know? The area settlers called “Yosemite” already had a name. Ahwahnee (ah-WAH-nee) Valley, which means “gaping, mouth-like place,” is the homeland of a number of Indigenous tribes, including the Ahwahneechee, Miwok, and Paiute people. A band of militia who violently removed many Indigenous peoples gave the area the name Yosemite. El Capitan and Yosemite Falls are two features of Yosemite Valley.
pages.brief: John Muir searches deep in the mountains for evidence that glaciers carved Yosemite Valley; he writes an article about glaciers, and other naturalists visit his Yosemite cabin, including Ralph Waldo Emerson; El Capitan and Yosemite Falls rise above the valley.

pages.text: Nature Writer and Activist After getting to know Yosemite so thoroughly, Muir devoted more time to writing about his experiences. In 1873, he moved to Oakland, California, and started writing magazine articles that made him famous throughout the United States. Muir wrote passionately, with the goal of investing his readers in natural spaces. In April 1880, Muir married Louisa (Louie) Strentzel and moved to her family’s fruit ranch in Martinez, California. Although Muir was a dedicated husband, he was unhappy with his responsibilities on the ranch. Always restless to be in remote places, he resumed his travels with Louie’s encouragement. Muir’s trip to Yosemite in 1889 resulted in the publication of two widely read articles about the area’s beauty and the importance of preserving it. Other people helped Muir by persuading Congress to protect Yosemite. These efforts to build public support on behalf of conservation were successful. The following year, Yosemite became the third U.S. national park, after Yellowstone and Sequoia. It was clear to Muir and other conservationists that an organization was needed to preserve Yosemite and other parts of the Sierra Nevada.
pages.brief: At a desk in Oakland, John Muir writes magazine articles about his experiences; later he stands with his wife Louie at her family's fruit ranch in Martinez, then walks through Yosemite, where his writing helps persuade Congress to protect the valley as a national park.

pages.text: Muir helped found the Sierra Club in 1892 and became its first president. The club’s purpose now includes protecting nature areas and wildlife throughout the United States. In 1903, President Theodore Roosevelt asked to meet with Muir to better understand the needs of remote nature areas in the West. Honored, Muir took him on a camping trip into Yosemite. Muir used the opportunity to advocate for setting aside natural lands as designated parks. As a result of that trip, more areas of Yosemite became part of the national park. Roosevelt also set aside many other natural spaces for protection, including Crater Lake and Wind Cave national parks. In his later years, Muir spent more time writing about his travels. He was awarded honorary degrees from four universities.
pages.brief: John Muir and President Theodore Roosevelt go on a camping trip in Yosemite, walking among tall trees and mountains as Muir urges protection for remote western lands; later, Muir writes at a desk and receives honorary degrees from four universities.

pages.text: Muir also led a twelve-year fight to protect Yosemite’s Hetch Hetchy Valley from being flooded by a proposed dam. Despite efforts to stop the project, including a letter Muir wrote to Congress, it was approved in 1913. However, the fight raised public awareness about the protection of natural lands. It also contributed to the 1916 creation of the National Park Service, which established stronger management for all U.S. national parks. John Muir died on December 24, 1914. Although he did not live to see the founding of the National Park Service, his efforts helped make it a reality. Do You Know? The word wilderness implies that a natural space is uncared for and uninhabited. Yet many of the spaces that Muir referred to as “wilderness” had been inhabited and managed by Indigenous peoples since before recorded history. Muir didn’t always understand or agree with Indigenous strategies for preserving the land. For example, while Indigenous peoples had been doing controlled burns— planned fires that keep a forest healthy—for thousands of years, Muir thought the only way to protect the land was to prevent any fires at all. Evidence now supports the effectiveness and importance of controlled burns.
pages.brief: Older John Muir writes a letter to Congress and stands before Hetch Hetchy Valley, a wild valley threatened by a dam; the dam is approved, and a forest scene shows controlled burns keeping the land healthy while public support for national parks grows.

pages.text: Many nature areas and establishments, such as Muir Woods National Monument, located north of San Francisco, bear John Muir’s name. The Sierra Club Today John Muir made significant contributions to environmental conservation in the United States. His devotion to protecting natural spaces led to the creation of national parks, which continue to preserve beautiful lands for future generations. Today, the Sierra Club focuses on a wide range of environmental issues throughout the United States, as well as global climate problems. The organization also works with Indigenous communities to protect the land and animals, ensuring the places we love to visit stay safe and healthy for years to come.
pages.brief: Tall trees stand in Muir Woods National Monument north of San Francisco; Sierra Club members work with Indigenous communities to care for land and animals, and people visit the protected forest, ensuring these places stay safe and healthy for future generations.

books.title: The Lakota
books.art_why: The book spans centuries of Lakota history and culture, including events where real photographs are impossible.

pages.text: The Oceti Sakowin Nation The Great Plains of the United States stretches from the Rocky Mountains in the west to beyond the Missouri River in the east, from Canada in the north nearly to Mexico in the south. The Lakota, who are part of the Oceti Sakowin (oh-CHEH-tee shah-KOH-wee) Nation, have a long history on the Plains. The Oceti Sakowin Nation is one of the largest Native nations in the United States today. It’s made up of three distinct groups based on language, culture, and geography: the Lakota, the Dakota, and the Nakota. Each of these is divided further into smaller bands. The Lakota make up the largest group in the Oceti Sakowin Nation. Before the 1800s, Native peoples made up a majority of the population of the Plains. Some lived in villages and grew crops. Others were nomadic; they moved around often, following the migration patterns of bison. The Lakota were one of the largest nomadic tribes. The Pine Ridge Indian Reservation, an Oglala Lakota reservation, in 1891.
pages.brief: The Great Plains from the Rocky Mountains to beyond the Missouri River, where Lakota people live as part of the Oceti Sakowin Nation. Show Lakota, Dakota, and Nakota groups, some in villages growing crops and some nomadic following bison. Include the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation in 1891.

pages.text: What’s in a Name? The Oceti Sakowin originally lived farther east on lands that are now part of Minnesota and Wisconsin. They were pushed westward in the 1700s by another Native group, the Ojibwe (oh-JIB-way). People outside the Oceti Sakowin commonly call them the Sioux (SOO), which may come from a term meaning “snake” or “enemy” in the Ojibwe language. Members of the Oceti Sakowin Nation refer to themselves as Lakota, Dakota, or Nakota, which all mean “allies, friends, or those who are united.” The Head of the Family Men and women traditionally had different responsibilities in Lakota society, but they were equally crucial to survival. Women were in charge of the family and the overall well-being of the group. They played an important role in making decisions for the good of the tribe. Women owned all the household goods, animals, and tipis (TEE-peez). It was their job to set up the tipis and take them down when the group moved camp. Women cooked and preserved food, collected water and firewood, made pottery and clothing, and raised the children. They often provided a majority of the food for the group by gathering wild plants and berries. They were also in charge of skinning the bison and cutting up the meat after a hunt.
pages.brief: Oceti Sakowin people moving west from lands now Minnesota and Wisconsin after pressure from Ojibwe. In a Lakota camp, women set up tipis, cook and preserve food, collect water and firewood, make pottery and clothing, raise children, and skin bison and cut meat after a hunt.

pages.text: Lakota women were admired for their artistic talent. They were very skilled at making clothes, shoes, and tipis from bison, elk, and deer hides. They made bison robes elaborately decorated with paint, porcupine quills, shells, and eventually beads. These robes took great skill to make and became very popular among European traders. Home on the Plains Like other nomadic Native peoples of the Plains, the Lakota once lived in tipis. These structures were ideal for life on the Plains. They could withstand strong winds, stay warm in the winter, and let air flow through in the summer. Wooden poles gave the tipi its cone shape, and bison hides were stitched together to make the walls. This design made it easy to quickly take down the tipi and carry it to a new place.
pages.brief: Lakota women making clothes, shoes, and tipis from bison, elk, and deer hides. They decorate bison robes with paint, porcupine quills, shells, and beads. Nearby, a cone-shaped tipi stands on the Plains, made with wooden poles and stitched bison hides, warm in winter and cool in summer, easy to take down and carry.

pages.text: Skilled Warriors and Traders Lakota men were highly skilled at handling and riding horses, which helped earn them a reputation as fierce warriors. Before the 1700s, the Lakota traveled and hunted on foot. Through trade and raids, they began obtaining horses, and by the late 1700s, the animals had become an important part of the Lakota culture and lifestyle. Lakota men reenacting a war party in 1907. Lakota men could gain wealth, honor, and higher status in their group through brave deeds and achievements in warfare. It was considered a great honor, for example, to be the first warrior to touch an enemy during battle. Capturing an enemy’s horse was also a great achievement. The Lakota were also talented merchants and traders who helped build a strong economy in the Plains. Because they were knowledgeable about the land and migration patterns of bison, Lakota hunters could acquire animal hides and furs much faster and more easily than European traders. They held fairs where they traded bison robes to Europeans in exchange for goods such as tools, beads, fabric, and weapons.
pages.brief: Lakota men riding and handling horses on the Plains, known as fierce warriors. Some men reenact a war party in 1907; others trade bison robes with European traders at a fair, exchanging for tools, beads, fabric, and weapons. A warrior touches an enemy or captures an enemy’s horse.

pages.text: Where Bison Roamed Tatanka (tah-TAHN-kah), or “bison,” are sacred animals to the Lakota and were crucial to the Lakota traditional way of life. The Lakota used every part of the bison. The bones were used to make tools, weapons, and everyday items, like paintbrushes. The horns were used to make cups, spoons, toys, and headdresses for ceremonies. The hair and fur were used in pillows, headdresses, and ropes. The hide was used to make robes, blankets, and tipis, among many other things. Bison were also the Lakota’s main source of meat. Before they had guns, Lakota hunters sometimes used bows and arrows to hunt bison. The Lakota were very skilled at hunting bison. Before they had horses, one hunting method the Lakota used involved luring a herd of bison over the edge of a cliff, causing the animals to fall to their death. This was very dangerous and required great skill, bravery, and teamwork. Today, bison are still very important to the religion and culture of the Lakota. Gifts made of bison products are prized possessions. A bison head or symbol is still used in almost every religious ceremony.
pages.brief: Lakota hunters using bows and arrows to hunt bison, or luring a herd over a cliff before they had horses. Show bison bones, horns, hair, and hides used for tools, cups, toys, headdresses, ropes, robes, blankets, and tipis. A bison head or symbol appears in a religious ceremony.

pages.text: Important Ceremonies Some of the religious ceremonies the Lakota performed hundreds of years ago are still performed today, though they may have changed over time. One of the most important is the Wiwanyang Wacipi (wee-WAHN-yahng wah- CHEE-pee), or the “Sun Dance.” The Sun Dance is held annually in late spring or early summer and lasts for four days. The Lakota build a hocoka (hoh-CHOH-kah), a ritual circle, on sacred ground for the ceremony. They place a tree in the middle that symbolizes the Great Spirit (or Great Mystery) and the center of the universe. Dancing takes place in the circle from sunrise to sunset, and as participants dance, they look at the sun. It’s a time of spiritual renewal of the Lakota’s relationship with the land and with all beings. Another important ceremony is Hunkapi (hoon-KAH-pee), or “Making of Relatives.” It was first used as a way to establish relationships and form alliances with other Native nations. Today, the ceremony serves as a way to join two individuals and their families together or for a family to formally adopt a child. The Lakota have been performing these and other ceremonies for centuries, but at one time, such ceremonies were forbidden.
pages.brief: Lakota people at the Sun Dance ceremony, dancing from sunrise to sunset inside a ritual circle on sacred ground, with a tree in the middle. Another scene shows Hunkapi, the Making of Relatives ceremony, joining two individuals and their families or formally adopting a child.

pages.text: War and Resistance Throughout the 1800s, the U.S. government tried to destroy the Lakota culture and religion, and force them to adopt the lifestyle and customs of European settlers. The government outlawed religious ceremonies and created boarding schools that Native children were forced to attend. Recognizing that bison were crucial to the lifestyle and spiritual practices of the Lakota, the government encouraged the mass killing of the animal. White settlers and soldiers killed millions of bison, taking the parts they considered valuable and leaving the bodies to rot and waste. The number of bison in the United States plummeted from about thirty million to only a few hundred by the end of the 1800s. Boarding Schools Beginning in 1860, the government and Christian missionaries established boarding schools for Native children where they were taught the customs and beliefs of white Americans. The children were forced to go to these schools, which were often far away from their homes. The children weren’t allowed to speak their own language, wear traditional clothing, or practice their peoples’ customs, and they were punished if they did. Many children didn’t see their family for years. Some never saw their families again. Native children attend math class.
pages.brief: U.S. government and Christian missionaries running boarding schools for Native children, far from their homes, punishing them for speaking their language or practicing customs. White settlers and soldiers kill millions of bison and leave bodies to rot. Native children sit in a math class at a boarding school.

pages.text: Lakota leaders signed many treaties, or agreements, with the U.S. government that established borders between U.S. territory and Lakota territories. However, because the U.S. government wanted to expand the country’s borders westward, it repeatedly broke these treaties, allowing white pioneers to settle on land that belonged to the Lakota. The Lakota were forced onto smaller and smaller areas of land called reservations. The government’s actions led to decades of war between the Lakota and the U.S. Army. One of the greatest victories for the Lakota against the U.S. Army during this time was the Battle of the Greasy Grass. After gold was discovered in lands sacred to the Lakota in 1875, the U.S. Army ignored previous treaties and invaded the area. Angered by this betrayal, thousands of Lakota people left their reservations and joined two Lakota leaders, Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse, in Montana. In June 1876, Native leaders learned of a coming attack on the camp by U.S. troops. Crazy Horse set off with around three thousand warriors to defend the camp. The U.S. troops were outnumbered and quickly overwhelmed. Within an hour, more than two hundred U.S. soldiers were dead.
pages.brief: Lakota leaders signing treaties with the U.S. government, then white pioneers settling on Lakota land as treaties are broken. Lakota people forced onto smaller reservations. In June 1876, Crazy Horse leads about three thousand warriors from a Montana camp to defend against U.S. troops; more than two hundred soldiers die within an hour.

pages.text: Because of skilled leadership, as well as the strength and dedication of their people, the Lakota achieved many victories in battle. However, continuous warfare, high death tolls, and the loss of crucial resources made it more and more difficult for the Lakota to defend their lands. Lakota leaders recognized that the only way to survive was to settle for peace and accept the terms of surrender, including moving onto reservations. Despite all this, the Lakota continued to preserve their way of life. They passed down their traditions and beliefs through oral history. They hid their children to protect them from being sent to boarding schools. They performed religious ceremonies in secret. Such efforts continued until 1978, when the American Indian Religious Freedom Act was signed into law, and the Lakota could once again practice their religion and customs in the open. A Lakota boy dressed in traditional clothing dances at a powwow in South Dakota.
pages.brief: Lakota leaders accepting peace and surrender terms, moving onto reservations, while Lakota people preserve traditions through oral history, hide children from boarding schools, and perform ceremonies in secret. In 1978 the American Indian Religious Freedom Act lets them practice openly. A Lakota boy in traditional clothing dances at a South Dakota powwow.

pages.text: Notable Lakota William “Billy” Mills (Tamakoce Te’Hila) 1938– Mills is a retired Olympic athlete. In 1964, he set a world record and became the first American to win a gold medal in the 10,000-meter race. Eagle Woman (Wambli Autepewin) 1820–1888 Eagle Woman was an activist, diplomat, and translator. She is the only woman to be recognized as a Lakota chief. Luther Standing Bear (Óta Kté) 1868–1939 Standing Bear was a musician and actor. He helped film studios hire Native actors and improve representation of Native culture in movies. Mary Brave Bird (Ohitika Win) 1954–2013 Brave Bird was an activist and author. She was a member of the American Indian Movement, which helped raise awareness about the treatment of Native peoples. Dr. Beatrice Medicine (Hinsha Waste Agli Win) 1923–2005 Dr. Medicine was an anthropologist, educator, and activist. She was an advocate for the rights of Native peoples. Tokata Iron Eyes 2003– Iron Eyes is an environmental activist. She travels all over the country to raise awareness about climate change. The Resilience of the Lakota Today, the Lakota continue to gather for festivals and ceremonies to celebrate and honor their heritage. Competitions and performances of traditional dances are held annually.
pages.brief: Portraits of notable Lakota: Olympic athlete Billy Mills, activist and chief Eagle Woman, musician and actor Luther Standing Bear, author and activist Mary Brave Bird, anthropologist Dr. Beatrice Medicine, and environmental activist Tokata Iron Eyes. Below, Lakota people gather at festivals and ceremonies with competitions and traditional dances.

pages.text: Lakota organizations have also revived once forbidden ceremonies for new generations. In the 1990s, the Brave Heart Women’s Society helped bring back the Isnati Awica Dowanpi (eesh-NAH-tee ah-WEE-chah doh-WAHN-pee), or “First Moon Ceremony.” This coming-of-age ceremony for Lakota girls is led by women in the community. Over the course of four days, girls learn about their culture and role as women and take part in traditional activities. The Lakota are also working to ensure younger generations learn their Native language. In 2007, Red Cloud Indian School, a Lakota school in South Dakota, partnered with Indiana University to create the Lakota Language Project. The program encourages the learning and use of the Lakota language in school and the community. The Lakota, along with more than sixty other tribes from nineteen states, are also helping to increase the population of bison in the Plains. Together, the tribes formed the Intertribal Buffalo Cooperative. Their goal is to restore bison populations in order to heal the land and the spirit of the Native peoples of the Plains for future generations. Since the creation of the organization in 1991, they have increased the bison population to more than twenty thousand.
pages.brief: Lakota girls taking part in the First Moon Ceremony over four days, led by women in the community, learning culture and their role as women. Students learn the Lakota language through the Lakota Language Project. Lakota people and other tribes work to increase bison populations in the Plains through the Intertribal Buffalo Cooperative.

pages.text: A young Lakota woman speaks at the United Nations Youth Climate Summit in 2019 (left). Students practice writing words in the Lakota language (top right). Young members of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe meet President Barack Obama (bottom right). Conclusion Despite war, discrimination, and a two- hundred-year campaign to destroy their way of life, the Lakota people and their culture have survived. Today, the Lakota continue to protect their ancestral land, increasing bison populations and organizing resistance to construction that would harm the environment. They work to teach younger generations and non-Native peoples about their history, language, and traditions. As teachers, doctors, activists, artists, and politicians, Lakota people continue to contribute not only to their own community but also to the world.
pages.brief: A young Lakota woman speaks at the United Nations Youth Climate Summit in 2019. Students practice writing words in the Lakota language. Young members of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe meet President Barack Obama. Lakota people work as teachers, doctors, activists, artists, and politicians, protecting land and teaching others.

books.title: The Amazing Undersea Food Web
books.art_why: Ocean animals and undersea zones exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Let Me Introduce Myself The ocean, where I live, is an enormous buffet table for everything in it and for many land animals, including humans. When you think of the ocean food web, you might think of fierce great white sharks devouring their prey, or enormous blue whales gulping tons of krill. Or you might think of giant stands of seaweed being devoured by everyone, like an underwater salad bar. But did you know that more than 90 percent of all sea creatures end up being eaten by other sea creatures? That means that almost every organism in the ocean ends up getting eaten by another sea creature at some point or other. And almost every sea creature eats other sea creatures.
pages.brief: Underwater view of a great white shark chasing prey and a blue whale gulping krill near tall seaweed stands, with many small sea creatures around them, showing the ocean as a busy feeding place where sea animals eat one another.

pages.text: These microscopic phytoplankton are called diatoms. But there are little organisms that almost always get eaten but do not actually eat anything themselves. They are the most microscopic species in the ocean, yet they form the center of the ocean’s food web. Some people might think it’s a raw deal to be food for everybody else, but I find it to be quite a powerful job. Let me back up and introduce myself properly. Phytoplankton (FY-tow-plank-ton) is my name. I’m an algae, which is almost like a very tiny plant. But unlike plants, I have no roots, so I’m not attached to the ground or sea floor. I’m free to float around with the ocean currents. I prefer to remain near the surface of the sea, since I’m quite fond of sunlight, and I can be found in every ocean on Earth.
pages.brief: Close microscopic view of tiny diatoms and free-floating phytoplankton drifting near the bright sunlit surface of the sea, with no roots holding them to the seafloor, spread through ocean currents in every ocean on Earth.

pages.text: Chlorophyll in plant cells absorbs the sunlight plants need to convert nutrients into food. Like plants, I make food through a process called photosynthesis, rather than eating it. I use chlorophyll to capture the Sun’s energy to change nutrients from seawater into food. Just as in plants, chlorophyll makes me green. But I’m so tiny that you can only see the color when there are billions upon billions of us in one place.
pages.brief: Tiny green phytoplankton cells in seawater use chlorophyll to capture sunlight and make food through photosynthesis, shown very close so their green color appears only where billions of them gather together in one bright place.

pages.text: A phytoplankton and zooplankton bloom shows up as light streaks in this photo taken from space. Fortunately, there are billions upon billions of us. Thousands of phytoplankton can be found in one cup of seawater. All that photosynthesis going on helps provide the Earth’s atmosphere with well over half of its oxygen. We are also a good indicator of the ocean’s health. Scientists can see large patches of phytoplankton from space. They can get information about the levels of pollution in the water when they see us struggling or dying off. But in my opinion, our most important job is providing the center of the food web for the entire ocean. We feed all ocean life forms directly or indirectly, from the smallest creature to the largest.
pages.brief: View from space of a phytoplankton and zooplankton bloom as light streaks in the ocean, with a cup of seawater holding thousands of phytoplankton, showing how scientists see large patches and judge the ocean’s health from above.

pages.text: The Food Web Here’s how it works: think about a simple tuna fish sandwich. Tuna are relatively large fish, and they eat smaller fish called mackerel. To make 1 kilogram (2.2 lbs) of tuna flesh, the tuna had to eat about 10 kilograms (22 lbs) of mackerel. Those 10 kilograms of mackerel had to eat 100 kilograms (220 lbs) of an even smaller fish called herring. And those 100 kilograms of herring devoured a full 1,000 kilograms (2,200 lbs) of zooplankton. Zooplankton are microscopic animals. They include tiny animals such as krill, which look like little shrimp, and the larvae and babies of crabs, jellyfish, shrimp, and other fish. To support those 1,000 kilograms of zooplankton, 10,000 kilograms (22,000 lbs) of phytoplankton were eaten. Tuna eat mackerel, which eat herring. Herring eat zooplankton, which eat phytoplankton.
pages.brief: Ocean feeding scene in the sea with a tuna chasing mackerel, mackerel chasing herring, herring eating zooplankton such as krill and larvae, and zooplankton eating phytoplankton, building a long food chain toward a tuna fish sandwich.

pages.text: This cross section shows the different zones of the ocean. To give you an idea of just how much life I support, I’ll take you through the ocean from the surface, where I live, down to the deepest trenches on the ocean floor.
pages.brief: Wide cross-section view of the ocean from the sunlit surface down through darker middle water to the deepest, dark trenches on the ocean floor, showing the different depth zones from the top to the bottom.

pages.text: Otters feed and live in the sunlit zone. Life in the Sunlit Zone The euphotic (yoo-FOE-tic) zone, or sunlit zone, is the top level of the ocean. It extends about 200 meters (660 ft) down from the surface. There’s lots of sunlight here, so we phytoplankton, along with ocean plants, love it. Consequently, most of the animal species in the ocean can also be found here. Red and green algae, also known as seaweed, cover much of the shallow ocean floor in the euphotic zone. Enormous giant kelp grow in thick forests, almost like forests on land, and provide shelter for many sea animals. Sea urchins live in the protected waters at the base of the kelp, and sea otters feed on those urchins. Sea otters also wind long strands of kelp around their bodies while they sleep in order to keep from drifting away.
pages.brief: Sunlit euphotic zone with thick giant kelp forests sheltering sea urchins at the base, a sea otter feeding on an urchin, and another sea otter sleeping while wrapped in long kelp strands to keep from drifting away.

pages.text: Almost all the seafood humans eat comes from the euphotic zone. Clams, mussels, and oysters live on shallow ocean floors. Lobsters and crabs scuttle about in coral reefs and among seaweed beds. Most species of fish, including salmon, tuna, mackerel, cod, and swordfish, stay up in the sunlight where there is plenty to eat and good light for hunting. Though there are squid and octopuses in the deeper zones, most of the ones that humans eat come from the euphotic zone.
pages.brief: Shallow sunlit ocean floor crowded with clams, mussels, oysters, lobsters, and crabs among coral reefs and seaweed beds, while salmon, tuna, mackerel, cod, and swordfish swim in the bright water where people catch most seafood.

pages.text: The euphotic zone is also home to coral reefs, which hold most of the ocean’s plant and animal species. These fragile and beautiful areas are formed by the accumulation of the skeletons of small animals called coral polyps. They are found in clear, tropical waters where there is lots of sunlight. Sea fans, brain coral, clown fish, angelfish, lion fish, moray eels, sharks, shellfish, crabs, and lobsters all make the coral reef a colorful and busy place. Anemones —animals that look like beautiful flowering plants—catch zooplankton with their stinging tentacles. Jellyfish swarm in massive numbers, attracting the sea turtles that love to eat them. Coral reefs also provide a safe haven for the young of many creatures that will live in the open ocean as adults.
pages.brief: Colorful tropical coral reef in clear sunlit water, with sea fans, brain coral, clown fish, angelfish, lion fish, moray eels, sharks, shellfish, crabs, and lobsters, an anemone catching zooplankton with stinging tentacles, and jellyfish swarming near a sea turtle.

pages.text: Humans love snorkeling and diving in the euphotic zone, especially around coral reefs. And they take thousands of tons of fish, both for food and for pets in tropical aquariums, from these surface waters. Unfortunately, all this human activity, along with pollution, threatens the well-being of coral reefs and other areas in the euphotic zone. Coral polyps are often killed by pollution, boat engines breaking them, or divers stepping on them, and once the corals die, all the other reef life suffers as well. Entire populations of fish can drop dangerously low from overfishing.
pages.brief: People snorkeling and diving around a coral reef in the sunlit zone, with a boat above and fish being taken from the water, while pollution and careless contact threaten the fragile coral and reef life.

pages.text: One nondestructive way to sample ocean life in the euphotic zone is to look into a tide pool. A tide pool is a small pool of water that remains when the tide goes out. You can find mussels, sea stars, urchins, clams, barnacles, and snails. You might even see an octopus, or you may spot a hermit crab scurrying about in another animal’s shell. You don’t even have to get wet to see all the life that depends, directly or indirectly, on me and my fellow phytoplankton.
pages.brief: Small wet tide pool left on the shore by the outgoing tide, holding mussels, sea stars, urchins, clams, barnacles, and snails, with an octopus nearby and a hermit crab scurrying about inside another animal’s shell.

pages.text: The Twilight Zone As you go below the euphotic zone, the water begins to get darker, colder, and heavier. You are now entering the twilight zone. It begins at about 200 meters (656 ft) and goes to a depth of about 1,000 meters (3,280 ft). The pressure in this zone would crush a person, but the life forms that live here have adapted to the pressure. The twilight zone, also called the disphotic (dis-FOE-tic) zone, doesn’t have enough light to support photosynthesis and plant life, but some animals do make their homes here. Others, such as whales, visit from the euphotic zone. Permanent residents include octopuses, squid, and strange-looking fish such as the hatchet fish and the viperfish. Many fish that live in this zone often have huge mouths with big, curved teeth. Because it is so hard to see, the fish don’t hunt. Rather, they simply hold open their fearsome mouths, waiting for something to swim in. Many of them are black or dark red to blend in with the dark water. This angler fish is small but scary.
pages.brief: Dark twilight zone below the sunlit water, with an angler fish, hatchet fish, and viperfish holding huge mouths and curved teeth, plus octopuses and squid in the cold, heavy water where animals wait for food to swim in.

pages.text: Sperm whales have sucker scars from fighting with giant squid. The famous giant squid also lives in this zone. Until fairly recently, no giant squid had ever been seen alive. The squids’ bodies occasionally washed up on shore or were found in the stomachs of sperm whales. Though a few people have seen it at the surface, and a few scientists have seen it in the disphotic zone, the giant squid still remains a mystery.
pages.brief: Deep disphotic water with a giant squid and a sperm whale bearing sucker scars from past fights, showing the mysterious squid that was long known only from washed-up bodies and whale stomachs and rarely seen alive.

pages.text: Many animals in this zone depend on a diet of what scientists call “marine snow,” which is a nice name for dead phytoplankton and zooplankton! When we die, our bodies drift slowly down through the ocean layers like snow falling through the air. So even where we don’t live, phytoplankton are eaten.
pages.brief: Tiny dead phytoplankton and zooplankton drifting slowly down through the dark ocean layers far below like soft falling snow, with small deep-sea animals feeding on the marine snow even where living phytoplankton do not live.

pages.text: The Midnight Zone This totally dark region of the ocean contains 90 percent of the ocean’s water, but almost none of its life. It extends from 1,000 to 5,000 meters (3,280–16,404 ft) and below. The pressure is so great that it can crush almost anything, including most submarines, and the temperature is near freezing. But there is some life in the midnight zone, or aphotic (ay-FOE-tic) zone, if you look closely. Many of the tiny animals that live here, such as the lantern fish, have little lights running up and down their bodies. The light comes from a special process called bioluminescence. This is the same process that produces light in fireflies. Jellyfish, squid, fish, and even bacteria are bioluminescent in this zone, where there is no sunlight. These lights make it possible for animals to see and communicate with each other. These lights also help them find mates or food, and they also make them incredibly beautiful. Some oceanographers divide the midnight zone into two additional zones: the abyssal zone and ocean trenches. The abyssal zone is totally dark, and it covers much of the ocean floor, including vast plains, mountains, valleys, and canyons.
pages.brief: Deep, cold, dark midnight zone with glowing lantern fish, jellyfish, squid, fish, and bacteria lit by bioluminescence, plus the totally dark abyssal zone below with vast plains, mountains, valleys, and canyons on the ocean floor.

pages.text: Ocean trenches occur along faults where large plates of the Earth’s crust come together. The colliding plates create canyons and cracks of up to 10,000 meters (32,808 ft) deep. You would think that nothing could survive at the bottom of a trench in the darkness, cold, and pressure. But openings at the bottom of the trenches spew hot water and minerals from deep within the Earth.
pages.brief: Deep ocean trench along a fault where huge plates of Earth’s crust collide, creating deep canyons and cracks, with hot water and minerals spewing from openings at the bottom into the darkness, cold, and pressure.

pages.text: Animals living in this zone have taken advantage of the warmth and nutrients. Special kinds of bacteria can use these nutrients in the same way that phytoplankton use sunlight. Tube worms, shrimp, and giant clams can all be found feeding on these bacteria around the openings, or chimneys. These chimneys were only recently discovered. Only a few submersibles, or submarines, have been built strong enough to withstand the enormous pressure at the bottom of a trench.
pages.brief: Deep trench bottom around hot chimneys, with tube worms, shrimp, and giant clams feeding on bacteria that use the mineral-rich water, while a small strong deep-sea submersible descends through the enormous pressure to observe them.

pages.text: Back on Top So you see, even though phytoplankton are only at the top of the ocean, we’re at the center of the food web, supporting all other life in the sea. Whether you enjoy the ocean for the beauty of coral reefs, the mystery of the abyssal zone, or some tasty fish and chips, you have us phytoplankton to thank.
pages.brief: Phytoplankton floating near the sunlit surface at the center of the food web, above a colorful coral reef and the dark abyssal zone, with a plate of fish and chips nearby to thank phytoplankton for supporting ocean life.

pages.text: (n.) page 10 the top ocean zone, which contains almost all of the ocean’s life faults (n.) page 20 cracks in Earth’s crust along which movement occurs photosynthesis (n.) page 6 the process by which plant cells absorb sunlight and use the Sun’s energy to transform water and carbon dioxide into food phytoplankton (n.) page 5 single-celled algae that live in a body of water snorkeling (n.) page 13 the act of swimming using a short, curved tube that extends above the water’s surface and allows the swimmer to breathe while under water submersibles (n.) page 21 small vessels that can operate underwater, especially at deep levels trenches (n.) page 9 cracks in the seafloor; long ditches zooplankton (n.) page 8 microscopic animals that live in a body of water.
